title: The right to development: Why equity, not charity, is a human right | UN News
authors: Daniel Dickinson, Shehzad Noorani, Lisa Hill, Hashim Azizi, Mulugeta Ayene
description:
Since 1986, the UN has recognised development not merely as economic growth, but as a human right that belongs to us all.
It encompasses economic, social, cultural and political rights aimed at reducing inequality and creating a fairer world.
This is precisely the “widening inequality within and among countries” that the UN’s human rights office (OHCHR) says the right to development exists to confront.
‘Inalienable human right’ The Declaration on the Right to Development (which is not a legally binding treaty) was agreed by UN Member States in 1986 and describes the “inalienable human right” to allow every person and people to “participate in, contribute to and enjoy” economic, social, cultural and political development.
The right to development “is not about charity, but enablement and empowerment”, the UN says.
text:
Neither chose their circumstances. Yet, one will likely live decades longer, earn far more and have a meaningful say in the decisions that shape their life.

The United Nations considers the gulf between those two children not simply unfair, but a violation of the right to development.

Since 1986, the UN has recognised development not merely as economic growth, but as a human right that belongs to us all.

It encompasses economic, social, cultural and political rights aimed at reducing inequality and creating a fairer world.

According to the World Inequality Report 2026, supported by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), half of the world’s poorest people own just two per cent of global wealth while the wealthiest 0.001 per cent – the billionaire class of around 56,000 people – hold three times more wealth than all of those poor people put together.

This is precisely the “widening inequality within and among countries” that the UN’s human rights office (OHCHR) says the right to development exists to confront.

‘Inalienable human right’

The Declaration on the Right to Development (which is not a legally binding treaty) was agreed by UN Member States in 1986 and describes the “inalienable human right” to allow every person and people to “participate in, contribute to and enjoy” economic, social, cultural and political development.

Crucially, it includes people’s sovereignty over their own natural wealth and resources.

Why does it matter?

The right to development “is not about charity, but enablement and empowerment”, the UN says.

Over the past 80 years since the end of the Second Word War, growth has not been shared equally and that inequality, left unaddressed, fuels poverty, unrest, migration and mistrust in institutions.

Key principles

People-centred development: The “human person” as subject and beneficiary of development

Participation: Active, free, meaningful involvement in decisions

Equity: Fair distribution of development’s benefits

Non-discrimination: No exclusion based on “race, sex, language or religion”

Self-determination: People should control their own resources

Do these principles really change lives?

Properly applied, the principles mean communities across the world do benefit.

In Morocco, vocational-training programmes are helping women launch income-generating activities.

Indigenous groups in Colombia have participated in the South American country’s peace accords.

In communities in Afghanistan, India and Palestine, people have learned how to share resources fairly rather than compete for them.

What happens when development leaves people behind?

The impact on people is just as concrete.

In Kenya, the Endorois, a community of roughly 60,000 people who had lived around Lake Bogoria for centuries, were excluded from the decision to turn their land into a game reserve. Denied consultation and a fair share of the reserve’s benefits, they lost the grazing pastures that were their livelihood, and large numbers of their cattle died.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, developing countries had less access to vaccines.

One UN official commented that “more than 600,000 deaths could have been prevented if all countries had been able to reach the World Health Organization vaccination target by the end of 2021. This failure was tragic and profoundly immoral.”

The barriers? Disagreement among States over binding obligations, weak international cooperation and a lack of political will are all holding back the right to development.

How relevant is it today?

Probably more relevant than ever before.

Climate shocks, conflict and immigration are overlapping global crises which are contributing to worsening poverty and inequality.

A fairer development system can help to reverse that trend.

Why is the UN focusing on this issue now?

It’s 40 years since the UN agreed on the 1986 Declaration on the Right to Development.

Member States will meet on 23 September at the UN in New York to renew the global commitment to ensuring that every person has a fair chance to live with dignity, opportunity and hope.

The meeting will bring together world leaders to reflect on progress made over the past four decades and to discuss how countries can work together to reduce poverty, expand opportunities and address inequalities that continue to prevent millions of people from fully benefiting from economic and social development.

title: USA and Brazil: Two Different Policies for Cuban Migration - Havana Times
description:
For decades, for the vast majority of Cuban emigrants, the United States was the destination of choice.
It is no secret that the Trump administration has made detention and deportation two pillars of its immigration policy.
For a community accustomed for decades to exceptional treatment under U.S. immigration policy, this shift threatens to overturn several deeply rooted assumptions.
In June, Brazilian police rescued 108 Cuban migrants in Roraima, on the border with Guyana, after they had crossed the northern border under precarious conditions.
Some difficulties facing Brazil Brazil has enough problems of its own to prevent any idealization.
text:
By Dario Alejandro Escobar (Joven Cuba)

HAVANA TIMES – Life can take many turns. Some of them, frankly, are almost impossible to predict. For decades, for the vast majority of Cuban emigrants, the United States was the destination of choice. The existence of the Cuban Adjustment Act, successive waves of migration, and a well-established community in Florida reinforced the idea that reaching US territory meant that, sooner or later, you would find a place where you could prosper. And in general, that was the case, but that image is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the scenes produced by Washington’s current immigration policy.

It is no secret that the Trump administration has made detention and deportation two pillars of its immigration policy. Beginning with the presidential campaign itself, Trump and his then vice-presidential candidate J.D. Vance warned that they would carry out mass deportations of migrants. In July 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) made 49,571 arrests, the highest monthly figure of Trump’s second term. More than half of those detained had neither criminal convictions nor pending charges. Detentions are no longer concentrated at the border; they are also taking place during traffic stops, routine immigration appointments, and operations in communities and public spaces.

At first, many Cubans believed that this rhetoric did not include them. For a community accustomed for decades to exceptional treatment under U.S. immigration policy, this shift threatens to overturn several deeply rooted assumptions. Since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second term, having relatives in the United States, having lived in the country for years, or being involved in an immigration process no longer guarantees that a person will remain beyond the reach of detention by ICE.

In any case, perhaps the most extreme expression of this policy is occurring far from the United States—and also very far from Cuba. Washington has turned to agreements with third countries to deport migrants to nations with which they have no previous ties. African countries such as Eswatini, Liberia, and Equatorial Guinea are among the main destinations for these deportations.

In August 2026, a group of deportees sent by the United States arrived in Liberia. Cubans were among them. The migrants refused to get off the plane, arguing that Liberia was not their country and that they feared for their safety. Authorities told them they would be returned to the United States. The plane, however, ultimately ended up in Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea, where they were forced to disembark. Reuters identified three Cubans among them, while El Nuevo Herald later reported that four Cubans were among the group involved in the transfer.

The case is part of a broader practice. Washington has signed agreements of this kind with several African countries, including Eswatini—formerly known as Swaziland—a small monarchy that has accepted migrants of other nationalities, including Cuban citizens. By the end of August 2026, more than 30 people had been transferred to that country under this mechanism.

The images speak for themselves. People who left Cuba seeking protection or better living conditions are being detained in the United States and then sent to an African country where they have never lived, have no family networks, and, in the vast majority of cases, do not even speak the language.

Social media has filled with testimonies from these people or their relatives asking for help or denouncing human rights violations by the current US government.

Deportations are only one part of the mechanism. Behind them is a vast structure designed to carry out this policy. Immigration facilities in poor conditions, allegations of abuse, transfers of detainees between different states without prior notification to them or their families, and legal proceedings that can drag on for months are all part of a system geared toward increasing the number of removals. For many Cuban migrants, the uncertainty that once ended upon arrival in the United States now continues even after they have crossed the country’s border.

There is also a major contradiction within the Cuban exile community itself. This policy is being carried out under an administration in which Marco Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants and current Secretary of State, holds one of the most powerful positions. In Florida, Cuban-American members of Congress such as Mario Díaz-Balart and Carlos Gimenez continue to fully support Trump and much of his agenda, while focusing much of their public discourse on tightening sanctions and increasing pressure on the Cuban government.

Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar has very timidly questioned aspects of immigration policy and has called for protection for Cubans with I-220A forms who have no criminal records. But it is nonetheless hypocritical for part of the Cuban-American political representation to denounce every arbitrary arrest in Cuba with tremendous intensity while that same energy is almost nowhere to be seen when Cubans are detained by ICE, held in poor conditions, or sent to third countries. Something similar occurs within part of the Cuban media and from influencers in the United States. Although deportations receive coverage, a narrative centered on “criminals” frequently predominates, while the impact of these measures on people without criminal records who emigrated in search of better living conditions is pushed into the background.

Brazil offers a very different picture

A Cuban citizen who is in or arrives in Brazilian territory can apply for recognition as a refugee through Sisconare, the Brazilian government’s digital system for registering and processing these applications. The application can then be formalized with the Federal Police. Applying for refugee status and being recognized as a refugee are two different things. It is up to the National Committee for Refugees (Conare) to analyze each case. While the application is under review, the applicant can remain legally in the country and obtain documents such as a Cadastro de Pessoa Física (CPF) tax identification number and a work card, as well as access rights and services provided under Brazilian law.

Migrants can also move freely throughout the country and access public services. Brazil’s Ministry of Justice itself recognizes the right of asylum seekers and refugees to healthcare, education, social assistance, and free legal aid. Access to the Unified Health System and public education does not depend on Conare having already decided to recognize that person as a refugee.

This is extremely important. It means that a person can arrive in the country, request protection, obtain documentation, and live like any other Brazilian citizen while waiting for the government’s response. And Cubans are making broad and extensive use of this avenue.

In 2025, Brazil received 75,599 applications for recognition of refugee status. Of these, 41,919 were submitted by Cubans. They represented 55.4% of the total, and for the first time Cuba surpassed Venezuela as the leading nationality among those seeking refuge in the country. The number of Cuban applications increased by 88.1% compared with the previous year.

The 2026 data confirm that the phenomenon is continuing. This year, Cubans and Venezuelans once again ranked among the leading nationalities seeking protection in Brazil. According to the Observatory of International Migration, Cubans consolidated their position as the national group filing the largest number of asylum applications in the country. It is estimated that more than 100,000 Cubans are already in Brazil with various types of immigration status. Many are even leaving the United States and flying directly to the South American giant.

The route, however, is not without danger. In June, Brazilian police rescued 108 Cuban migrants in Roraima, on the border with Guyana, after they had crossed the northern border under precarious conditions. Five suspected human traffickers were also arrested. Following the operation, the Cubans were referred for immigration regularization procedures and assistance services.

It is important to clarify that there is no need to cross illegally into Brazil. Any migrant can arrive at a border checkpoint and request asylum from the Federal Police. They will not be deported.

In other words, when faced with an undocumented or vulnerable migrant, Brazil’s first approach is regularization. In the United States, amid the current immigration crackdown, even a person who entered legally through programs such as humanitarian parole may face detention and removal to another continent.

That said, this does not mean that obtaining Brazilian documentation is a panacea.

Integration is probably where Brazil still has a considerable debt to pay. The right to work exists on paper, but finding formal, well-paid employment can be more difficult. University degrees earned in Cuba must undergo recognition procedures that can be lengthy, expensive, and bureaucratic. Professionals trained as doctors, engineers, teachers, or journalists can spend years working in jobs completely unrelated to their qualifications.

Portuguese is another barrier. Although Spanish and Portuguese share many similarities, facing a job interview, pursuing university studies, or seeking skilled employment requires a command of the language that cannot be acquired immediately upon arrival in the country.

Brazil should develop broader Portuguese-language programs for immigrants that are directly linked to employment integration. It could also create faster and less expensive mechanisms for recognizing professional skills and degrees. In addition, it would be useful to strengthen connections between asylum seekers and companies that need workers, offer specific guidance for entrepreneurs, and better incorporate municipalities and states into integration policies.

Cuban migration has characteristics that make it possible to consider more specific policies. There are qualified professionals with experience in services, healthcare, education, tourism, and other fields. Cuban communities are growing in various Brazilian states, and this population could integrate more successfully if the government moved beyond simply guaranteeing documentation and also helped facilitate social mobility.

The case of the Federal University of Paraná, in Curitiba, is proving to be a successful model in this regard. There, several Cuban and Latin American professionals are able to obtain a Brazilian university degree through credential-recognition procedures offered by the institution. This is an example that should be replicated in every state in the country.

Some difficulties facing Brazil

Brazil has enough problems of its own to prevent any idealization. It has high inequality, informal employment, racism, xenophobia, and a bureaucracy capable of turning a simple procedure into months of waiting. Asylum also does not in itself guarantee economic stability or definitive recognition of refugee status. Nevertheless, while the United States intensifies immigration detentions and resorts to third countries to deport Cuban citizens, Brazil allows thousands of them to request protection and remain legally in its territory while their cases are evaluated. And that difference says a great deal about how the two countries understand the protection of migrants, many of whom are fleeing a context of profound crisis that makes it practically impossible to build a dignified life.

One country places those it says it “wants to save” inside a machinery increasingly geared toward mistreatment and expulsion. The other still faces serious shortcomings in terms of integration, but provides them with documents, authorizes their access to the labor market, and recognizes their human rights from the very beginning of the process. And so far, this has not depended on whether the government is on the right or the left; it is a state policy. Even under the previous government, which was on the far right, Cubans and other migrants found conditions in Brazil that allowed for reception and regularization.

For those who are already building their lives outside Cuba, or considering the possibility of emigrating, this contrast is worth taking into account.

They can choose between a destination where arrival may mean a detention center and another where it begins with documentation, access to employment, and rights recognized from the outset.

Everything seems to indicate that, at last, our north is becoming the south.

At least for a while.

First published in Spanish by Joven Cuba and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

text:
KANSAS CITY, KS —A Latino civil rights organization filed an appeal Friday of a federal court decision ending access to regular tuition rates for students without lawful immigration status who formerly qualified under Kansas law.

MALDEF (Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund) and co-counsel filed the appeal on behalf of Kansas Students for Affordable Tuition (KanSAT), an association of college students without lawful immigration status who relied on Kansas’ tuition policy to afford higher education.

“Absent some recent change in applicable law, duly-enacted state legislation should never be struck down without full and complete consideration of all legal arguments,” said Thomas A. Saenz, MALDEF president and general counsel. “That did not happen here; Kansas students who relied on a state law that is over 20 years old in enrolling in Kansas colleges and universities deserve their day in court.”

On Sept. 9, U.S. District Judge Holly L. Teeter of the United States District Court for the District of Kansas denied KanSAT’s motion to intervene in a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) challenging Kansas’ tuition-equity law. The court also denied Governor Laura Kelly’s motion to intervene. Finally, the court entered the consent judgment sought by the DOJ and Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach. The judgment bars Kansas from enforcing the state law that allowed certain students without lawful immigration status who met specified requirements to qualify for regular tuition rates at public colleges and universities. Along with the notice of appeal challenging the denial of intervention, attorneys also filed a protective notice to preserve KanSAT’s right to challenge the consent judgment.

“The district court’s denial of intervention leaves members of KanSAT in a precarious situation of incurring high levels of student debt or leaving their respective program altogether,” said Luis Lozada, MALDEF staff attorney. “Rather than grapple with the intervention motion, the district court improperly adopted the reasoning of another circuit court; KanSAT filed an appeal in order for the Tenth Circuit to consider KanSAT’s meritorious arguments that align with precedent.”

Since 2004, Kansas law has allowed certain students without lawful immigration status who attended and graduated from Kansas high schools and met other requirements to qualify for regular tuition rates at public colleges and universities. MALDEF filed its motion to intervene on behalf of KanSAT on July 1, after the DOJ sued Kansas and sought to invalidate the law on the basis of a federal law on the books since 1996. The same day the DOJ lawsuit was filed, Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach joined the federal government in asking the court to invalidate the law rather than defend it.

In their motion to intervene, attorneys argue that KanSAT’s members pursued higher education in Kansas in reliance on a decades-long promise that they would qualify for regular tuition rates. If those guarantees are eliminated, students could face thousands of dollars in unexpected tuition costs each semester, threatening their ability to complete their degrees. Many come from low-income families and are ineligible for federal financial aid, leaving them with few options to absorb the sudden financial burden. Some may be forced to take on significant debt, delay graduation, or withdraw from school altogether.

“We applaud the students in Kansas and their courage in speaking up for their future,” said Jessica Swonger, Staff Attorney for the ACLU of Kansas. “The Department of Justice, in collusion with Attorney General Kobach, should not be able to trod on the rights of hardworking Kansas students, and we will not stop fighting for educational opportunity.”

The appeal was filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

A notice of appeal was filed in the District Court for the District of Kansas by MALDEF, joined by co-counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union of Kansas.

MALDEF is also representing students challenging the elimination of regular tuition rates in Kentucky, Oklahoma, and Texas.

text:
The Supreme Court has ordered the Government to pay a Westmoreland woman over $11 million after it found that immigration authorities violated her constitutional rights when they took her off an outgoing flight in Kingston and confiscated her passport for more than seven months.

Jacqueline Dahlia Thompson was awarded $6 million in compensatory damages and $5 million for vindicatory damages after the court concluded, at the end of her lawsuit, that a number of her constitutional rights were breached by the Passport Immigration and Citizenship Agency (PICA) during and after the November 2024 incident.

Vindicatory damages are typically awarded by the courts to underscore the gravity of a breach of a citizen’s fundamental constitutional rights.

Thompson, who was heading to Mexico for medical treatment at the time she was removed from the flight, was also awarded special damages of US$2,762 to recoup out-of-pocket losses for airline ticket and hotel accommodation.

The Attorney General’s Department (AGD), which represented PICA, did not file a defence explaining why Thompson’s passport was confiscated and held for approximately 230 days before it was returned.

The AGD, however, filed legal arguments asking the court to adopt the approach taken in a similar case decided in 2023 and award Thompson “nominal damages” of $1.5 million for breaches of her right to due process, the right to leave Jamaica and the right not to be deprived of a passport.

“In the absence of a defence from the defendants [PICA], it can be concluded that breaches of the right to be granted a passport and not to be denied or deprived thereof, the right to leave Jamaica and the right to due process of law have been engaged,” an attorney from the AGD acknowledged in the filing obtained by The Sunday Gleaner.

Justice Lisa Palmer Hamilton found, in a ruling delivered on Thursday, that confiscating the passport on November 15, 2024 and keeping it until July 3, 2025 without a hearing, a formal charge against Thompson or “a clear explanation” breached a number of constitutional provisions.

The right to due process of law

The right to equitable and humane treatment by a public authority in the exercise of its functions, the right to due process of law, the right to hold a passport and to travel outside Jamaica were among the provisions cited.

Thompson claimed, in her lawsuit filed by attorneys Peter Champagnie, King’s Counsel, and Neco Pagan, that on November 15, 2024 she was on board an Arajet flight destined for Mexico where she was scheduled to undergo a medical procedure.

However, the businesswoman, who lived overseas and recently relocated to Jamaica, said she was removed from the plane by immigration officers in what she described as “embarrassing and humiliating” circumstances.

The passport was seized by an immigration field officer who directed her to visit PICA’s head office on Constant Spring Road, in St Andrew.

Thompson claimed that during a visit three days later, she was interviewed by the same field officer who explained that “a photograph said to resemble her had been used on some earlier passport application”.

The businesswoman said she immediately and “unequivocally” denied any knowledge of such applications and explained that all her prior passport renewals were processed through the Jamaican Consulate in New York City.

She noted that no criminal charges were filed against her arising from the allegation made by the immigration field officer, but still her passport was not returned even after two letters from her attorneys.

The passport was returned on July 3 last year after the lawsuit was filed.

However five days later, immigration officers again removed Thompson from an outgoing flight at the Norman Manley International Airport, the lawsuit claims.

She was allowed back on the plane after her attorneys contacted PICA’s legal office.

text:
September 20, 2026 - New York — Make the Road New York, the New York Legal Assistance Group (NYLAG), and the Association to Benefit Children (ABC), and African Communities Together (AFT) filed a lawsuit against U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) seeking to vacate an unlawful new rule that will, beginning September 18, deny lawful permanent resident (LPR) status to aspiring immigrants because they or their dependent children receive supplemental public benefits. Plaintiffs are represented by Democracy Forward, the Legal Aid Society, and the Center for Constitutional Rights

Plaintiffs allege that the new rule and related guidance violate the Immigration and Nationality Act, which has long reserved a public charge denial for a very small percentage of individuals who are likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence. Instead, the new rule and guidance are designed to punish immigrants, including their children, for receiving even small amounts of nonmonetary supplemental benefits for which they are eligible.

The benefits encompassed by the new policies include health insurance, food assistance, housing assistance, benefits for children like the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children and Head Start, benefits for workers like the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, and even Pell grants for college students. None of these benefits, used by citizens and non-citizens alike to build financial security and independence, relate to the type of long-term destitution Congress recognizes as making someone a public charge.

The new policies also give DHS officers unbridled discretion to deny aspiring immigrants LPR status on public charge grounds. The rule is also a barely disguised cover for the administration’s racial animus towards non-citizens and their children. The rule will create a massive chilling effect on the lawful, necessary, and appropriate use of public benefits by noncitizens, whether or not they are even subject to the rule, and by their U.S. citizen children.

The reduced access to public benefits is likely to lead to a range of harmful effects on immigrant communities and the public at large, including worse health outcomes, higher prevalence of communicable diseases, as well as increased rates of poverty, food insecurity, housing instability, and homelessness.

“With this rule, more than double the number of New Yorkers will have to choose between receiving benefits that keep a roof over their heads, access to medical care and food on their tables or their ability to become a legal permanent resident,” said Julie Brandfield, Director of New York Legal Assistance Group’s LegalHealth Unit. “Every year, our medical-legal partnership clinics serve nearly 9,000 hospital patients whose families choose to navigate through the complex immigration system and a web of benefits bureaucracy so that they can continue on their journey to becoming healthy and secure Americans. This new rule change will not only harm the cancer patient fighting for their life or the older adult seeking care as they age; it will also harm our organization’s ability to give legal advice and services that ensures the best outcomes for the futures of thousands of New York families.”

Rebecca Telzak, Co-Executive Director of Make the Road New York, said, “The extreme changes to the public charge rule will cause irreparable harm to our country’s health and public services. The Trump administration has actively worked to advance policies that further their anti-immigrant agenda and bar immigrants from being able to apply to any immigration benefit. Despite the rule changes not yet in effect, we have witnessed the chilling effect on immigrant communities, and even among those who are categorically exempt or will not be impacted, their fears have led to questioning unnecessary disenrollment from critical public benefits. At its core, this new rule is cruel: at a time when the cost of everything—from food to housing to healthcare—is unbearably high, immigrant families and U.S. citizen children will be punished for accessing these basic necessities.”

“This rule is about more than status; it denies our community members access to healthcare, food, and housing, at a time when people across the country are struggling to have their basic needs met,” said Diana Konaté, Deputy Executive Director of Policy and Advocacy at African Communities Together. “The rule forces families to choose between maintaining a secure status and visiting the doctor. This is an inhumane and costly decision for our country and will have detrimental long-term effects broader than the immigrants it targets.”

“No family should have to forgo putting food on the table, getting healthcare, or keeping a roof over their heads because they are pursuing a lawful path to permanent residency,” said Skye Perryman, President and CEO of Democracy Forward. “Yet that is exactly the unlawful and cruel choice the Trump-Vance administration is trying to force on immigrant families across the country. Congress did not give this administration the power to punish people for accessing supplemental supports for which they and their children are eligible. We are honored to represent our clients alongside our partners in challenging this policy and protecting families and communities from its devastating consequences.”

“Tens of thousands of households across the United States currently receive assistance from the government to supplement their wages in this challenging economy,” said Susan Welber, Supervising Attorney at The Legal Aid Society. “USCIS and DHS’s new rule to deny LPR status to aspiring immigrants solely on the grounds that they or their U.S. citizen children receive any form of non-cash government assistance is both wrong on the law and a blatant attempt to bar low-income immigrants, particularly immigrants of color, from becoming permanent residents. This illegal rule, like the 2019 rule, must be vacated by the court to ensure that all aspiring immigrants remain free to live in the United States and pursue economic success for themselves and future generations without sacrificing the health and well-being of themselves, their families, or their communities.”

“The rule is inspired by the tiresome and repeatedly debunked notion that racial minorities disproportionately use public benefits and will drain the nation’s coffers,” said Angelo Guisado, a Senior Staff Attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights. “We are all now bearing witness to the Trump administration’s vindictive crusade to remake the United States. Time and again we see that it is the poor, the Black and Brown, or the immigrants who suffer most — here it is a trifecta.”

The case is Make the Road New York et al. v. USCIS et al., and the legal team at Democracy Forward includes Ryan Cooper, Joel McElvain, and Elena Goldstein.

Read the filing here.

description:

The Justice Department, meanwhile, has denied that it is preparing to send agents to polling places.
"This time, it is the federal government ordering ICE and other federal law enforcement to intimidate naturalized citizen voters and immigrant communities.
In 2026, voters should not have to choose between their safety and their right to vote.” NAACP general counsel Kristen Clarke said the threatened deployment would turn polling places into "militarized zones."

text:
A coalition of civil rights and labor groups led by the NAACP sued the Trump administration Friday in a bid to prevent armed federal agents from being deployed at or near polling places during November's midterm elections, warning that the threatened presence of such officers could intimidate voters of color and repress turnout.

The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia by the NAACP, National Urban League, Mi Familia en Accion, OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates, SEIU, American Federation of Teachers, International Union of Painters, and United Food and Commercial Workers International.

The complaint names senior Trump administration officials as defendants, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel, and White House border czar Tom Homan. The lawsuit seeks an order barring the administration from "deploying agents in a manner that unlawfully intimidates voters or anyone urging or aiding voters."

The plaintiffs are represented by the Legal Defense Fund, Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund (AALDEF), Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law, LatinoJustice PRLDEF, National Immigration Law Center, Protect Democracy, and Democracy Defenders Fund. They argue that the administration's policies and statements have created a reasonable fear among Black, Latino, Asian American, naturalized, immigrant, and mixed-status voters that they could face questioning, surveillance, detention, or force while voting.

Asked in May whether he would send National Guard troops or ICE agents to polling locations, President Donald Trump refused to rule out such a move, saying that he would “do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”

Other senior administration officials have similarly refused to rule out the deployment of federal forces to polling places in the name of fighting voter fraud—which is extremely rare.

The Justice Department, meanwhile, has denied that it is preparing to send agents to polling places. Spokesperson Kiersten Pels called such suggestions "fearmongering," while Mullin has said ICE would not patrol polling locations.

The coalition is suing under Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits intimidation, threats, or coercion of people for voting or attempting to vote, as well as those assisting others in voting.

“All American voters have the sacred right to have a voice in our democracy, and should be able to exercise that right freely and without fear,” said Janai Nelson, president and director-counsel of the Legal Defense Fund.

“Using federal law enforcement as a scare tactic to target and intimidate Black communities is illegal and antithetical to the promise of a multiracial democracy that was enshrined in the Voting Rights Act," Nelson added. "Neither Black, Latino, Asian, or any other voters nor any other communities should ever again face the threats of terror and intimidation at the ballot box that defined the Jim Crow era.”

“We are experiencing a level of voter intimidation like we haven’t seen since the civil rights era."

AALDEF executive director Bethany Li asserted that "when the federal government puts fear between people and the ballot box, that is voter intimidation—plain and simple."

“We are experiencing a level of voter intimidation like we haven’t seen since the civil rights era, when local governments and the KKK openly intimidated Black voters," Li added. "This time, it is the federal government ordering ICE and other federal law enforcement to intimidate naturalized citizen voters and immigrant communities. In 2026, voters should not have to choose between their safety and their right to vote.”

NAACP general counsel Kristen Clarke said the threatened deployment would turn polling places into "militarized zones."

"Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn't protection and it isn't oversight; it's disenfranchisement, period," she argued.

The lawsuit comes one week after a similar challenge was filed by the League of United Latin American Citizens, UnidosUS, Common Cause, and the city and county of Denver, Colorado. That case cites an 1865 federal law that generally prohibits federal officials from bringing "troops or armed men" to places where elections are being held, except when necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.

text:
A US Federals Court has ruled that immigrants facing deportation to third countries must be given sufficient notice before being sent to nations where they have no ties.

A US federal appeals court has ruled that immigrants facing deportation to countries where they have no ties must receive sufficient notice and a meaningful opportunity to challenge their removal before being sent there. A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit unanimously struck down a Department of Homeland Security policy that allowed the administration to deport immigrants to so-called third countries with little or no advance notice. The ruling means migrants must be allowed to raise concerns if they fear persecution or other harm in the country to which they are being deported. “An individual's right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” Circuit Judge Seth Aframe wrote in the ruling.

What are third-country deportations?

A third-country deportation involves removing an immigrant to a country that is neither their country of citizenship nor necessarily a country where they have family or other ties. The Trump administration has expanded the practice in recent months after reaching agreements with dozens of countries, including Liberia, Ghana, the Central African Republic and Sierra Leone. About 25,000 people have been deported to third countries during the administration's immigration crackdown. The administration has cited diplomatic assurances from receiving countries that deported immigrants will not be mistreated. But the lawsuit challenging the policy argued that migrants were sometimes given little or no opportunity to object before being put on flights to countries where they could face persecution or other serious harm. The appeals court agreed that prior notice and an opportunity to challenge the destination were required. The Washington Post reported that the court found the government had not adequately shown which countries had provided the diplomatic assurances relied upon by the administration. The case follows reports of immigrants being deported to countries they had never visited. ABC News recently reported on a group of Latin American men sent to the Central African Republic who said they were not told their destination until hours into the flight. The latest ruling does not eliminate the government's ability to deport immigrants to third countries. Instead, it requires the administration to provide the procedural protections migrants need to challenge removal to a particular destination before sending them there. The ruling is the latest development in a broader legal battle over the Trump administration's expanded use of third-country deportations.

title: People taken into custody by ICE in Arkansas recall life in Louisiana detention site
description:
Tahay, Garcia-Medina and another detainee who spoke to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette described a world inside Winn's walls far removed from the one from which they'd been pulled.
*** After arriving at Winn, Garcia-Medina met Meslier Salinas, a pastor from the same hometown in Nicaragua who by then had been detained for about two months.
Winn has been a dedicated ICE detention facility since 2019, according to federal records.
Separated by detention, Enriquez and his wife joined their children in conversation through calls made simultaneously with cellphones on speaker placed next to each other.
* * * The water was only one of the problems at Winn, Enriquez and others said.
text:
WINNFIELD, La. -- The stillness is broken by the footsteps of two guards. They walk down a hallway and stop briefly in front of each cell. From a list, they read the names of the men who will be deported that night.

Each day, between 11 p.m. and midnight, the ritual occurs inside the Winn Correctional Center in north-central Louisiana. The droning of soccer and news television broadcasts is interrupted. The chatter of detainees playing cards fades. Fifty to 60 men rush toward a fence facing the main hallway.

"It was always the quietest moment. We all wanted to get out of there," said Jose Garcia-Medina, 47, of Chinandega, Nicaragua, who lived in Fort Worth while seeking asylum. He said he was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement during a regularly scheduled check-in in Dallas before being brought to Winn.

From October 2022 to August 2026, more than half the people taken into ICE custody in Arkansas spent the longest stretch of their detention in Winn, according to ICE data processed by the University of California, Berkeley's Deportation Data Project and analyzed by the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette.

More than 60% of those detained in the men's only facility during that period had never been convicted of a crime, the data show.

"I had never been arrested before. I had never been to a place like this," said Eugenio Tahay, 28, a native of Guatemala who was detained while driving from Little Rock to Clarksville, Texas, to see his wife, Karla, and bring his 2-year-old son, Mateo, a bag with new teddy bears and toy cars.

Tahay, Garcia-Medina and another detainee who spoke to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette described a world inside Winn's walls far removed from the one from which they'd been pulled. Water stained yellow and brown flowed from faucets and shower heads. The men ate hard rice and dry beans. Some food was served rotten or undercooked. They became constipated and ill.

They sought to mount legal defenses knowing the odds against them were staggering. Of those who left the lockup this year through August, 97% were deported.

In the meantime, Tahay and the others were left to contemplate their fates, awaiting the sound of the steps and the call of their names.

"There was a clock on the wall, but it felt like time never moved," Tahay said.

* * *

Tahay's wife didn't answer his nightly call from Winn on Feb. 19.

He anxiously phoned his sister-in-law in Arkansas. Hours later, a policeman showed up at the hotel where Karla had been working and living with the couple's son and her mother. A niece translated, communicating largely in Quiché, the Mayan language spoken in Ixcán, the northern Guatemalan town from which the family hails.

Twenty minutes till 6 p.m., the time when Tahay regularly called her, Karla was in a fiery crash on a Clarksville, Texas, highway, Tahay said. Colleagues tried to pull her from the flames. She was already dead, Tahay said.

"Some days I didn't eat because of the sadness," Tahay said. "I always gave myself to God and asked him for strength, and strength for my son, mother-in-law and family."

He spent eight months in Little Rock after moving from Houston for a job building metal framing at construction sites. His wife stayed behind, working at the hotel in northeast Texas, 20 miles from the Oklahoma state line. Tahay never got to utter a final farewell to his bride.

When he told the guards at Winn, they asked that his mother-in-law write a letter saying her daughter had died, Tahay said. He provided copies of his wife's death certificate and his American-born son's birth certificate at their request, he said, but nothing changed.

"As much as I asked for help, for a way to at least say goodbye to her body, the detention guards never gave me any support," Tahay said.

He spent his days reading the Bible and playing cards, unable to shake the shock of his loss and his despair of being unable to care for his son.

"They never helped me with anything," Tahay said. "In the end, they just deported me."

* * *

The sprawling Winn Correctional Center complex sits on a 300-acre plain surrounded by towering pines and the Kisatchie National Forest in Winn Parish.

Detainees from Arkansas, Texas, Alabama and other states are transported in white vans down an undulating rural road lined by white wooden signs featuring red numbers counting down the miles to the facility's gates. The markers warn drivers against recording and photographing.

On the west side of the complex, its main entrance, a red brick building with a beige-colored roof serves as the entry point for detainees and visitors. Past the first checkpoint, rimmed by about a mile and a quarter of barbed wire, sit 10 buildings of varying size and materials. Five large X-shaped units house an average daily population of more than 1,300 men, according to Maryland-based research group Relevant Research, based on its analysis of ICE's publicly released data.

From October 2023 through July of this year, the number held at Winn peaked in February at more than 1,600.

***

After arriving at Winn, Garcia-Medina met Meslier Salinas, a pastor from the same hometown in Nicaragua who by then had been detained for about two months. An asylum seeker, Salinas was apprehended in December during a regular check-in at an ICE office in Little Rock. Garcia-Medina soon learned of conditions already familiar to Salinas.

"Sometimes I would eat nothing but the bread," Garcia-Medina said.

The water caught detainees' attention. Before drinking a cup, they said, they heated the water in a microwave in an effort to drive out bacteria.

"Water in Winn is always brown," said Adrian Enriquez, who said he was detained on New Year's Eve 2025 along with his wife, about 1,500 feet from the couple's Winnfield home.

"That's how you have to drink it," said Tahay. "There's no other way."

Occasionally, guards would provide a bucket of ice. The cubes were brown too, Enriquez said.

During a January inspection by ICE's Office of Detention Oversight, detainees complained about the color of the water, according to a federal report.

Office of Detention Oversight inspections are announced to the facility four weeks in advance, the report says. Inspectors spend two to three days on site.

"Several detainees reported a yellow tint to the drinking water and shower water," the report reads. Inspectors "observed the facility's water and observed it did have a yellow tint."

An assistant warden provided inspectors with the most recent annual water test report, dated June 2024, which found the facility "met all federal and state health-based standards for human consumption," the report says.

Detainees were "dissatisfied" with that explanation, the report says. No action taken to correct the problem was given in the report.

* * *

Technology and machinery replaced the labor that men like George Moss once provided at a local plywood mill as part of the once-thriving timber industry in the community surrounding the detention center.

"In a poor parish like ours, in a poor region, " said Moss, the former mayor of Winnfield, "nobody thinks technology can affect the timber industry, but what used to be a 30-man logging team is now three."

"It's all automated now. All those jobs are gone," he added.

He was the fourth employee at Winn when the facility opened in 1990. The state owns the lockup. A warden manages daily operations and support staff. LaSalle Corrections, a Louisiana-based private prison company, manages the facility, food services and medical care. Winn has been a dedicated ICE detention facility since 2019, according to federal records.

ICE stations deportation officers there. The Winn Parish sheriff's office provides detention, transportation and guard services under a federal contract. The U.S. government pays the sheriff's office for the service, but a copy of the contract obtained by the Democrat-Gazette redacted the amounts.

"The prison has been a great asset for the entire region," said Moss, who worked there until 1992.

Neighbors echoed the sentiment.

"The jobs are there," said Gail Kelley, 77, a retired school nurse in Winn Parish who rides her bicycle near the detention center. "It's in a safe spot. It's convenient."

Since President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown began, she said, she's noticed an increase in traffic as detainees are shuttled in and out of the facility.

"You see buses coming every day," Kelley said. "And the buses are always so blacked out, you never know who's on there, so it does not affect us at all."

* * *

Enriquez had been inside Winn for a month when he saw a man he'd known since moving to Winnfield from nearby Natchitoches in 2005. The guard, who is also Hispanic, and Enriquez attended the same church. Their families were friendly with one another. Enriquez said he approached the man and extended a hand. The guard turned away.

"I called him by his name," Enriquez said, "and he didn't answer."

Since the early 2010s, Enriquez' mother and other relatives had worked at El Patio, a local Mexican restaurant.

With his parents gone, Angel Arellano, Enriquez' 17-year-old son, washes dishes and buses tables at El Patio starting at 5 p.m. He begins his days 12 hours earlier at a welding shop before classes for his senior year of high school. He gave up football to help his older brother support their two younger brothers, who are 16 and 11. After school, he joins a maintenance crew for which his father once worked.

His and his family's faces are familiar in Winnfield, Enriquez said. Some guards recognized him from the restaurant and were friendly.

"I saw many of them graduate high school with my oldest son," Enriquez said. "Many of them spent nights at my house. I fed them."

Eventually, the guards he knew were no longer seen in his cell area, Enriquez said.

Separated by detention, Enriquez and his wife joined their children in conversation through calls made simultaneously with cellphones on speaker placed next to each other. He said Angel offered to drop out of school and work full-time to support his brothers.

"What hurts the most is seeing them work so much," Enriquez said. "It makes me feel like when I left my mother here in Mexico to search for that dream of doing better."

* * *

The water was only one of the problems at Winn, Enriquez and others said.

Rice and macaroni were often undercooked and hard to chew, they said. Chicken was so burnt it dried detainees' mouths. In other cases, the chicken was uncooked, Enriquez said.

"Sometimes the chicken they'd give you was raw," Enriquez said. "You were going to get sick."

When he complained to guards, Enriquez said, they shrugged.

Instant mashed potatoes, a staple in their meals, were often so watered down as to be transparent.

"Why would a mashed potato be clear?" Enriquez said.

Federal inspectors found perishable food stored in freezers with temperatures 20 degrees warmer than the recommended limit.

ICE later provided the Department of Homeland Security inspector general's office with photocopies of logbooks "demonstrating facility staff were monitoring coolers and freezer temperatures daily to ensure they were within the required temperature ranges," the report says.

Detainees also worried about the threat of violence. After guards pepper-sprayed a detainee in the hallway in front of Garcia-Medina's cell, he said, he drenched his white T-shirt in the yellow water and wrapped the garment around his face to avoid breathing in chemicals.

A trove of use-of-force incident reports leaked to The Washington Post included seven 2024 cases at Winn involving the use of pepper spray. It isn't clear from what the Post published how many times pepper spray was used after mid-January 2025.

Reviewing five use-of-force incidents at Winn, federal inspectors found three in which staff violated standards.

Those cases included staff applying a chokehold to a detainee, failing to document a medical review and its findings on camera and puncturing a detainee's skin with a pen to gain compliance, the inspectors' report says.

* * *

Lists of lawyers' phone numbers were posted on walls inside the detention center, Garcia-Medina said. When he called some of the names using his commissary money, he said, every answer he got was in English.

"Even if they gave you the option of pressing 1 or 2 for Spanish, they'd still only answer in English," he said.

Garcia-Medina, like all other detainees interviewed for this story, was interviewed in Spanish by the Democrat-Gazette.

The facility is required by law to provide detainees with easy access to legal materials by prominently posting an official list of local, free legal service providers, according to an inspector general's report.

Inspectors found those lists at Winn were outdated, incomplete or missing entirely. The facility only has four local, free legal service providers for a population of more than 1,500 detainees, inspectors noted.

The report said ICE responded that "updates on legal material and law library information were made and posted on bulletin boards in every housing unit, law library, and program area throughout the facility. ICE also stated staff issues Zip drives to detainees upon request."

The inspector general's office said ICE had not shared any evidence that the legal information had been publicly posted around the facility.

Detainees said they increasingly felt like there was no way back.

"At first I had hope," Garcia-Medina said. "But I ended up resigning myself to knowing I was going to be deported."

* * *

The night Garcia-Medina thought his deportation had come, he called family in Nicaragua to let them know he would be arriving that day.

About 4 a.m., he said, he was taken from his cell and loaded onto a bus the same way he had arrived, with his wrists, waist and ankles chained. He was driven to the airport in Alexandria, La., where he sat waiting on the bus for hours, he said.

After about 12 hours in chains with only a sandwich to eat, he said, he and about 10 other men were driven back to Winn. He said a guard told him the plane had no room for them.

"To me that's bad coordination, but also psychological abuse," Garcia-Medina said. "They completely played with me."

On the night Enriquez was deported, he said, he used another inmate's commissary money to call his family.

He was loaded onto a bus with tinted windows. He peered out at the familiar sights of the town that had been his home for more than two decades.

Angel said he sped to the local McDonald's, where he had seen detention vans pass. About 10 other relatives joined him waiting for a glimpse of the bus that would take Enriquez from Winnfield.

Angel said he hoped his father would see the bright lights they had installed on his truck together and hear its loud engine.

But it was too late. The bus sped past the McDonald's at about midnight, before the family arrived, Enriquez said.

The family waited until about 4 a.m., Angel said. He never saw his father.

Enriquez was deported to Mexico in May after more than 25 years in the U.S.

On April 27, a month after his first trip to the airport, Garcia-Medina was deported to Nicaragua after four years in the U.S.

Tahay, who had lived in the U.S. for a decade, was deported April 11.

name: Agencies
title: Detainees contend Oklahoma ICE site is neglecting medical care | Exclusive
authors: Maria Guinnip , The Oklahoman, NATHAN J. FISH, THE OKLAHOMAN
description:
Families and attorneys said they were unable to visit some of the earliest Diamondback detainees virtually or in-person.
ICE booking process delays access to hygiene products, medication For many advocates, the biggest concern is medical care.
Officials tour Diamondback, attorneys question access to medical care Secrecy surrounding the facility has compounded the questions about its operations.
When asked about access to care, Gustin said everyone detained at Diamondback has "daily access to sign up for medical care."
This article originally appeared on Oklahoman: Detainees contend Oklahoma ICE site is neglecting medical care | Exclusive Reporting by Maria Guinnip , The Oklahoman / Oklahoman USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Copyright Reuters or USA Today via Reuters Connect
text:
Valentina Timaran Restrepo had a mass growing in her abdomen that went untreated for weeks, leaving her in constant pain that worsened every day.

Timaran Restrepo was being detained at the privately-operated Diamondback Correctional Facility in Watonga. Records say federal agents had taken her into custody as she attended a routine immigration check-in. She had immigrated to the United States from Colombia.

Medical staffers at the detention center ordered an urgent ultrasound to pinpoint what was causing the mass to grow. But she was told the ultrasound could take up to one month to receive. It required outside approval.

The mass swelled and pressed against her abdomen. She had trouble moving and sitting. According to court documents, she had to be taken to the emergency medical unit at the facility on a near-daily basis.

She petitioned a federal judge to intervene. The judge ordered staffers to take her to the hospital April 1 and provide all necessary care.

Timaran Restrepo is one of at least 16 people detained at Diamondback who have sought temporary restraining orders to get medical care they say they urgently need. One of the largest facilities for ICE detention in the country, Diamondback reopened to accommodate a surge in arrests under a nationwide federal immigration crackdown.

The true number of detainees who have alleged medical neglect at Diamondback is likely much higher than publicly known, because a majority of immigration court documents are sealed.

Timaran Restrepo is still being detained at Diamondback. Her case is one of few filed by detainees where the judge's orders were made public. She argued that waiting one month was "medically untenable," and that if she did not receive care she was at risk of "life-altering damage."

A federal appeals court has ruled that court action in such cases are "an extraordinary remedy," requiring the right of relief to be "clear and unequivocal." Timaran Restrepo argued facility operators knew she needed urgent care and failed to ensure it, effectively turning her "regulatory detention into unconstitutional punishment."

Advocates for people detained at Diamondback say as the facility received an influx of detainees from across the region, conditions worsened. Detainees, their families and their attorneys described difficulties receiving timely medical attention and prescribed medications as routine, alongside concerns about nutrition and unsanitary conditions.

"It's so degrading," said Brenda Lozano, an associate attorney at Rivas and Associates, an immigration law firm. "You just can't live – that's not a sustainable way, that's not a healthy way to live, and that's why people are sick."

Operated by Tennessee-based CoreCivic, Diamondback had been empty since 2010 and was reopened in December 2025 after the Oklahoma Department of Corrections signed a five-year contract on behalf of ICE to resume operations at the 2,160-bed facility. CoreCivic has said it expects to earn $100 million a year operating the facility. It also runs several other ICE detention centers across the nation.

Families and attorneys said they were unable to visit some of the earliest Diamondback detainees virtually or in-person. At the time, CoreCivic cited temporary construction as hindering accommodations for in-person attorney visits. Company representatives say construction has since been completed.

Attorney Elissa Stiles said that while client call access has improved, her concerns have grown about the living conditions within the facility. She is the senior lead attorney at the Tulsa office of Rivas and Associates, which represents dozens of people who have been detained at Diamondback.

"None of my clients seem to be physically well," Stiles said. She described her clients as looking weak, losing weight and being "in a fragile place, physically."

Stiles said some of her clients have also described the food as undercooked or lacking nutritional value, leaving them to go hungry, as well as lights remaining on throughout the night, making it impossible to sleep.

Lozano said the food often consists of little protein. They have also received complaints regarding the water at Diamondback, "there's particles floating around," she said.

In a statement provided to The Oklahoman, CoreCivic spokesperson Ryan Gustin disputed concerns about living conditions, including access to medical care and clean water. Gustin said detainees are provided three nutritious meals every day and drink the same water as CoreCivic employees.

"Claims that individuals are routinely denied necessary medical treatment or prescription medications are inconsistent with our policies and practices," Gustin said.

Neither ICE nor its parent agency, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, responded to questions from The Oklahoman about conditions within Diamondback.

Complaints mount about conditions at Diamondback, other ICE facilities

Travis Handler, a legal fellow at the ACLU of Oklahoma, said he receives anecdotal and anonymous reports about conditions within Diamondback from the American Bar Association. Many of the reports echo what immigration attorneys have also heard.

"The reports that we have seen consistently that are most troubling are lack of access to adequate and timely medical care, the lights being on virtually at all times – which makes it really difficult to sleep." Handler said, "Complaints about bad or rotten food, lack of access to potable water. I've heard reports of feces and urine running over in toilets, no privacy in the bathrooms."

The concerns aren't isolated to Diamondback. Across the country, people being held in federal immigration detention have reported getting sick after consuming food that was spoiled, infested with bugs or not fully cooked, along with concerns about access to potable water and hygienic resources.

At Dilley, a CoreCivic run Texas detention facility for immigrant families, parents reported finding cockroaches in their food and said their children were vomiting after drinking the tap water. And at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in Southern California, fly larvae were found in water samples after growing claims of water contamination.

In July, a federal judge ordered immigration officials to make immediate changes to improve the health and safety of detainees in response to a lawsuit alleging inhumane conditions at Adelanto. The judge ordered ICE to provide adequate medical care and 24-hour access to clean drinking water, in addition to meeting other basic needs.

In Oklahoma, Handler described the concerns as widespread and consistent, saying he has compiled more than 25 complaints about Diamondback from a variety of sources, with all of the reports concerning food quality, medical care, access to counsel or limited access to recreation time.

ICE booking process delays access to hygiene products, medication

For many advocates, the biggest concern is medical care.

Attorneys with Rivas and Associates have filed multiple requests for temporary restraining orders, seeking immediate medical care for clients detained at the Watonga facility who detailed neglect. Not all of the orders have been granted.

"The only cases we've seen go to the hospital is when it's been court-ordered or life-or-death," Lozano said.

Many issues arise during the booking process, which can last up to a week, Stiles said. Detainees have reported sleeping on mats and not having access to medications, even if they had brought them on hand or in a bag at the facility.

As a practicing immigration attorney, Sen. Michael Brooks-Jimenez, D-Oklahoma City, said he could confirm from his own experience with clients at Diamondback and other facilities that intake can be uncertain, with clients sometimes being stuck. He said throughout this period, clients frequently do not have access to medicine or communication devices until they are processed into a pod or regular housing.

"Perhaps there is a black hole there," he said.

Rep. Arturo Alonso, D-Oklahoma City, said he has also heard concerns from family members whose loved ones are currently detained. One person reached out for help saying her relative had epilepsy was not getting the medication she needed, he said.

The situation is not uncommon. Attorneys say clients have reported not receiving their daily prescriptions for issues such as high blood pressure, diabetes and heart conditions.

Attorneys at Rivas & Associates described an incident in early summer when more than 50 people were transferred at once from Dallas. While waiting to be processed into the facility, the detainees reported not being provided with basic hygienic resources, such as a towel or soap to shower, for a week. People became sick.

"Those individuals were left in a waiting room that didn't have enough beds or blankets or people didn't even receive fresh clothes," Lozano said. "This waiting lasted for three weeks before people were accommodated to an actual room."

Gustin said CoreCivic provides necessities, such as clothing, blankets and toiletry kits. "Suggestions that individuals generally are not provided basic hygiene items or necessities are inconsistent with facility practices," he said.

Officials tour Diamondback, attorneys question access to medical care

Secrecy surrounding the facility has compounded the questions about its operations.

Brooks-Jimenez has visited the facility twice since Diamondback reopened. For both of his visits, Brooks-Jimenez went on a four-day notice in his capacity as an elected official and said everything seemed clean throughout his tour.

In early July 2026, U.S. Sen. James Lankford, Oklahoma's senior Republican senator, posted a video from outside of the facility's walls in western Oklahoma after what he described as a "full access" tour. He said he had met with medical professionals and toured visitation areas, housing pods, the kitchen and dining area.

In his video posted to social media he said, "It's exceptionally well-run, and it's a facility that's set up to be able to actually enforce American law."

Lankford declined to comment for this story.

When elected officials have toured the property, they have all said they met with medical professionals on-site. Immigration attorneys worry that - based on the first-person accounts they are hearing - professionals are not as accessible as they seem.

"To our knowledge there isn't someone on-site who is available and accessible every hour of the day for emergencies," Lozano said. "If there is, there might be just limited capacity, because we have several clients who haven't received the immediate care that they've requested, and especially in urgent situations."

Sarah Daquioag, a staff attorney at Rivas & Associates, said clients who are too sick to get out of bed are told that they need to go seek medical attention themselves, rather than have an attorney intervene on their behalf.

When asked about access to care, Gustin said everyone detained at Diamondback has "daily access to sign up for medical care." The care includes mental health, dental care and prescription management, if needed.

He also said providers "meet the highest standards of care, as verified by multiple audits and inspections."

The Oklahoma State Health Department inspects all city and county detention facilities at least once every year, but because Diamondback is privately operated, it does not fall under the same purview. In his statement, Gustin described the Watonga facility as being monitored by partners at ICE, while all facilities are subject "independent audits without prior notice."

A search of job listings shows CoreCivic hiring for dozens of positions at their Diamondback facility, primarily for medical positions including a licensed practical nurse, primary care physician, psychiatrist, psychologist, medical records clerk, registered nurses, health services administrators, clinical supervisors, mental health therapists and specialists, and a recreation supervisor.

In response to questions about whether the facility was adequately staffed, Gustin said Diamondback was "staffed to support the safe management of the facility and the delivery of required services."

"Like many organizations nationwide, correctional and health care providers continue to face workforce recruitment and retention challenges," he said.

Gustin said the facility has "grievance, medical and reporting channels" in place to address individual concerns.

Lozano said some people fear retaliation if they report their concerns.

text:
The surging U.S. immigration crackdown since 2025 has negatively impacted Latino businesses in Los Angeles, home to the country's biggest Hispanic population, where increases in federal arrests of migrants have led to fewer customers and lower sales.

Teodoro Cuevas, a Mariachi musician who has come to the Mariachi Plaza in Boyle Heights -- a cultural hub for Los Angeles' Latino community -- to play music for 25 years, is one of many workers and business owners feeling the effects of a major expansion in immigration enforcement.

"There used to be a lot of people here. The mariachis were here, dressed and ready to work every day. The work isn't the same anymore," he said.

Federal immigration arrests nationwide reached nearly 51,000 in August, a record for a third consecutive month.

In Los Angeles County, business owners say greater enforcement has spread fear through Latino neighborhoods.

A study by the Latino Policy and Politics Institute at University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) found the June 2025 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids led to 46,000 fewer customer visits and more than 3 million U.S. dollars in estimated losses near nine immigration enforcement sites in the two weeks after the operations, including the Fashion District, an iconic commercial and cultural landmark of Downtown Los Angeles.

"Before, there were so many people you could barely walk. Now, there's more space and fewer people," said Eric Vaquero, a fabric store worker.

Leonardo Crespo, owner of a restaurant in Boyle Heights, said he used to serve about 100 customers a day, but the figure is now closer to 20 in some days.

"The concern about other people, it's just getting hauled in, because you look a certain way. That's it. It doesn't matter. I had my mother telling me. 'You should carry your birth certificate.' I said I'm not going to do that," he said.

Those concerns are not limited to undocumented immigrants. A ProPublica investigation documented more than 170 U.S. citizens held by immigration agents in the first nine months of 2025.

At least 53 people died in ICE custody between the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term on January 20, 2025 and mid-July 2026, according to a joint report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.

"So, if you are a Hispanic person that even was born in the U.S., a citizen, you may be scared of going out, because ICE has big pressure to detain people, and they are known for being hostile. So you actually fear for your life or safety or think 'I don't want to be detained.' Right?" said Julio Sevilla, a professor at University of Georgia.

The ongoing China-ASEAN Expo serves as a bridge for China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to boost trade flows, helping both sides reap shared development dividends.

Scheduled to run from Sept 17 to 21 in Nanning City of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, the event draws more than 3,400 exhibitors from over 70 countries and regions.

This year, Timor-Leste is participating for the first time as a full ASEAN member and a co-host of the expo, with participants noting results have exceeded expectations, bolstered by China's vast market.

"I brought 60 packages of 250-gram coffee, which would be sold out in one day. Now I'm thinking that China market is open for everybody and it's very huge," said an exhibitor from Timor-Leste.

Participants also hailed the construction of China's Pinglu Canal, which officially opened to traffic on Wednesday.

The 134.2-km-long canal runs from Hengzhou, a county-level city in Guangxi, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.

The canal becomes a cost-competitive river-sea intermodal shortcut connecting ASEAN producers with the vast consumer market in southwest China, said the participants.

"In the past, shipments into the southwest China usually went by sea to Guangzhou and then overlands. Too many handover made it hard to keep products fresh. Losses were high and transit time was unreliable. Now that the canal is open, we can enter [the] Guangxi [Zhuang Autonomous Region] directly from the Beibu Gulf and move on to Yunnan, Guizhou and Sichuan restaurants, faster onto the supermarket shelves and tables in the southeast [part of China]," said an exhibitor from Vietnam.

With the formal signing of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area (FTA) 3.0 Upgrade Protocol in Oct 2025, bilateral cooperation has expanded beyond economic and trade areas to emerging fields such as the digital economy and the green economy.

"I am looking for an investor to develop agriculture and integrated tourism with us in Malaysia," said an exhibitor from Malaysia.

Economic ties between China and ASEAN have continued to deepen. Bilateral trade topped 1 trillion U.S. dollars for the first time in 2025, totaling 1.05 trillion dollars, up 7.4 percent year on year. In the first seven months of 2026, trade between the two sides reached 744.41 billion dollars, an increase of 24.7 percent year on year and accounting for 21.8 percent of China's total foreign trade.

China has remained ASEAN's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has been China's largest trading partner for six successive years.
