name: Litigation
title: For those detained during Operation Midway Blitz, release doesn't mean freedom
authors: Andrew Carter, Laura Rodríguez Presa, Gregory Royal Pratt, Caroline Kubzansky
description:
In the 11 months since his detainment during Operation Midway Blitz, he’d learned to live without much of either.
For immigrants without legal status, release is often framed as a victory.
Some will seek legal status through family members who are U.S. citizens or permanent residents.
Like many who were detained only to be released, Cazares needed a combination of luck and legal might.
Walter Pascual said he tried for years to obtain legal status after he entered the country in 2005 from Guatemala.
text:
Freddy Cazares arrived at his lawyer’s office in Pilsen a few minutes early on a gray Thursday morning in August, ready to sign the documents that he hoped might provide some measure of security and peace. In the 11 months since his detainment during Operation Midway Blitz, he’d learned to live without much of either.

His release early last December, he said, had been “like a miracle.” It came after 80 days locked away, first in the Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing center in Broadview — where “they treated us worse than animals,” he said — and then in a jail about 200 miles south, in rural Clay County, Indiana.

For most of his detainment, he waited to be flown out of the country. He’d signed deportation papers under duress, he said, and when agents drove him and other detainees from Broadview to an airport he waited for his name to be called. But then the plane filled and he never heard his name, and “they put us back in a van and took us to Indiana.”

Almost three months later, a judge ordered his release. Cazares, 38, had been praying for it. He has a wife. Three American-born children. No criminal record. He’d crossed the border from Mexico as a teenager and eventually settled in Wheeling. The United States has been his home for more than 20 years. Whatever elation he felt upon his release, though, proved fleeting.

Cazares entered into a prolonged limbo that could end in deportation anyway. In the Chicago area, he was among nearly 3,800 immigrants who were arrested and detained during Operation Midway Blitz, according to a Tribune analysis of ICE data provided by the research group Deportation Data Project. Among those, more than 1,000 ultimately won their release.

They soon learned that didn’t necessarily mean freedom.

For immigrants without legal status, release is often framed as a victory. In reality, it is usually temporary, conditional and far from secure. Years can pass before an initial court date. A final resolution can take much longer.

Operation Midway Blitz, one year later

Some, like Cazares, are granted parole. They may even receive work permits. The reprieve allows them to rebuild their lives — however temporary — while their cases slowly drag through a backlogged court system. But immigration attorneys say release may simply mean continuing court proceedings outside detention before deportation.

“The release in and of itself is about human dignity and due process,” said Jennifer Babaie, the associate director of the Adult Detention Project at the National Immigrant Justice Center. “But it is just one step on a still Herculean effort to try to go through all of the legal loopholes you need to try to retain any kind of legal status here.”

For many, a release isn’t necessarily a new start. It is instead part of a long goodbye.

**

Cazares begins most days at sunrise and works construction or as a day laborer throughout the city and suburbs. He would have rather been working the morning of his appointment the first week of August but instead arrived a few minutes before 10:30 and walked through the doors of the Pilsen branch of The Resurrection Project, a Chicago nonprofit dedicated to immigrant advocacy.

He brought his 14-year-old nephew to help translate, if needed, and one of his sons. Cazares looked nervous as he took a seat and waited. Much of the past year has been one long test of his perseverance, and there is no way to know when it all might end. Or where.

A door swung open and Elizabeth Suarez, a paralegal, called his name. He followed her up a narrow stairway and into a small office with block glass windows that allowed light but no view, and he took his seat on the other side of her desk. A stack of papers awaited and Suarez walked him through the forms and the boxes that required his signature.

“Make sure everything is in order,” she said, speaking to Cazares in Spanish. “Please double-check your name every time. It’s with a Z, right? I always forget. Phone number. Your current address.”

“Si,” Cazares said quietly, thumbing through the documents.

“So, if everything looks good, please sign here,” Suarez said.

He signed the forms and Suarez made copies and that was it. An appointment of about 10 minutes.

If all went to plan Cazares would receive a work permit in the mail, and it would offer a layer of protection. It was another step to show he was trying to do the right things, along with the scheduled check-ins with ICE and avoiding even the most minor of run-ins with the law.

The largest question, though, hung over him:

Would he be allowed to remain in the country that has been his home for 22 years?

Those who are released, and want to stay, experience similar uncertainty while they navigate contrasting legal journeys. Some will fight asylum cases. Others will continue visa applications. Some will seek legal status through family members who are U.S. citizens or permanent residents.

For Cazares, detainment created a pathway that otherwise would not have been available, said Peter Meinecke, senior staff attorney at The Resurrection Project. Some like Cazares, who’ve been in the U.S. at least 10 years, are eligible for cancellation of removal. If an immigration judge grants Cazares the order, he can obtain lawful permanent residence.

That creates a complicated situation, Meinecke said, because detention can ultimately give someone access to a form of relief for which they could not previously apply. Losing the case, though, could also result in deportation.

“If you don’t win, then you run the risk of getting a removal order,” Meinecke said. “If you win you get a green card.

“It’s really fascinating to me. Like who created this incomprehensible system? It’s insane.”

**

Cazares won his release like many — if not most — who were detained during Operation Midway Blitz: through habeas corpus, a 200-year-old American legal doctrine that has surged as a defense strategy amid President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement operations.

Habeas corpus, which allows a defendant to challenge the legality of their imprisonment, is among several mechanisms for release, some of which depend on a detainee’s location. In some cases, a release might come through a judge who grants bond. In others, ICE can grant bond, or parole.

Unlike criminal cases, in which a person may be able to post a percentage of the bond, an immigration bond generally must be paid in full before release. The costs vary widely and depend on several factors, said Katherine Greenslade, managing director of The Resurrection Project.

“They look at how long they’ve been here,” she said. “Do they have U.S. citizen or legal permanent resident family? What sort of community ties do they have?”

Those released often receive a check-in appointment within a few weeks, Meinecke said, and must meet conditions — wearing an ankle monitor, for instance, and keeping documentation — while their cases continue. A violation can lead to re-detainment.

In February, a little more than a month after his release in Clay County, Indiana, Cazares was back at an ICE facility. This time at the Office of Enforcement and Removal Operations for a check-in to determine, again, whether he would be allowed to pursue a case or be forced to leave the country.

His hands trembled as he walked into a large room with gray chairs against tall white walls. “Deport voluntarily,” one sign read. The same message was posted in nine languages.

He sat and leaned his head against the wall.

“Ojalá todo salga bien. Que sea lo que Dios diga,” he said, praying: I hope everything goes well. Whatever God wills.

A young ICE agent appeared and asked a boy who’d accompanied Cazares to translate a message.

“Basically, he is out on parole. So no traffic violations or anything like that, and you won’t hear from us,” the agent said as he handed Cazares a document with the information. Cazares smiled with relief. His next check-in is scheduled for January 2028.

He folded the paper and put it in his wallet.

**

He considered his release a miracle because of its improbability. Like something divine. Like many who were detained only to be released, Cazares needed a combination of luck and legal might.

He expected to be deported. He’d signed the papers during a confinement in Broadview that he described as harrowing: detainees sleeping on the floor and next to toilets; officers imploring Cazares and others to sign away their lives in America to go back to their home countries, no matter how long it’d been since those countries were home.

“They said if I didn’t sign, they would punish me,” Cazares said.

Not long after signing, Cazares boarded a bus to the airport, where he waited for a moment that never came. At least not for him. At the jail in Clay County, he contacted his wife for the first time since his arrest. She connected him with Andrés Díaz, an attorney from The Resurrection Project.

Among Díaz’s first questions for Cazares was this: Do you want to accept deportation? Or do you want to fight? Until then, Cazares believed he was destined for deportation, or worse.

“I thought I was going to die in there,” he said.

**

Until recently, immigration attorneys used habeas corpus only on rare occasions. It used to be reserved for people navigating prolonged detainments in extreme, outlier cases.

But then the second Trump administration began and, with it, the immigration enforcement operations that swept over the country and arrived in Chicago with militant force. As the Broadview detention center filled, and while federal agents moved detainees from there to jails in Indiana and Kentucky and elsewhere, habeas corpus emerged as a viable legal tool.

“It’s only really under this new administration where it’s just become this absolutely necessary prerequisite to get pretty much anyone out of detention,” said Carlos Estrada, a senior litigation attorney from the Illinois Habeas Project for the National Immigrant Justice Center.

Operation Midway Blitz came with the promise of targeting the so-called “worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens” in the city. Quickly, it became clear that agents instead targeted anyone who appeared to be Latino.

Cazares was installing siding during a job in Naperville when he was detained. And like him, the vast majority of those arrested during the blitz had no criminal record.

“We’ve seen them pretty much indiscriminately pick up anyone and everyone without a warrant, without probable cause, including people who they themselves had released on parole or on an order of supervision,” Estrada said. “For most of these folks, the government could process their cases without detaining them.”

Successful habeas petitions do not necessarily lead to quick resolutions. For those detained in the blitz and released, the average stay in custody lasted 2 ½ months. Those released often found themselves far from where they were detained. Cazares needed a friend to pick him up in Indiana. Some in Broadview had been sent to facilities in Texas and Arizona.

For Cazares, and many who decided to fight their cases, detainment represented the beginning of the effort to gain legal status. Cazares in June applied for a form of relief known to immigration lawyers as “non-LPR cancellation of removal” — LPR an acronym for lawful permanent resident.

In addition to the 10-year residency requirement, applicants need a clean criminal record, and to have been “a person of good moral character.” The final requirement is perhaps the most difficult to meet: They have to establish that “removal would result in exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” for family members who are U.S. citizens.

The thought of being separated from his children haunted Cazares. It also pushed him to fight.

“I couldn’t even get out of bed anymore,” he said. “The only thing that kept me going was seeing my children again.”

At home after his release last Dec. 8, the relief gave way to long-term anxiety. His children have been “suffering,” he said, and their grades have gone down. He has told them to focus while his case continues. He has told them that all they can do is to move on and keep going.

But Cazares doesn’t know where he’s headed, exactly.

“I got out of that hell, but it still feels like it’s out here,” he said.

The outcome of any given relief case is “very judge dependent,” said Meinecke, of The Resurrection Project, and while he believed in Cazares’ case he acknowledged the uncomfortable truth: There were hardly any guarantees.

A green card, deportation, another detainment — they all remain possible. While Cazares tended to his paperwork during his August visit, Meinecke and a few others worked in a small space upstairs. The “endless cycle,” as he put it, of detainments and delayed releases and far-off court hearings had made for busy times for immigration lawyers.

It also left people in legal purgatory. Cazares’ far-off next court date, not until 2028, is not atypical, Meinecke said, given the backlog of cases in the fallout of the blitz.

“This is all a result of a broken system,” he said. “Like, a decades-long broken system.”

**

The system is a maze in which laws collide with gray areas, where layers upon layers of policy have accumulated over decades in a pile waiting for reform that has never come.

“The fact that it doesn’t make sense is entirely consistent with the history of the U.S. immigration system,” said Nicole Hallett, a clinical professor of law and director of the Immigrants’ Rights Clinic.

It is a system that has created a paradox, and led to a large population of undocumented immigrants who lack a straightforward path to permanent legal status. The laws that limit their entry in the first place “have not discouraged people from coming,” Hallett said.

“But it has meant that the undocumented population has grown over time because it’s very difficult to legalize your status once you’re here.”

The tension is particularly clear in temporary immigration programs. Temporary Protected Status, for example, provides protection from removal, and work authorization to eligible nationals of designated countries under certain circumstances.

But it does not provide a path to lawful permanent residence or citizenship. The Department of Homeland Security has acknowledged that some have remained in TPS for decades.

The problem with temporary status is not simply that it is temporary, Hallett said. It is what happens when people build permanent lives while living under a temporary designation.

The U.S. has repeatedly attempted to overhaul its immigration system, but reform has failed to become law despite major legislative efforts. Hallett, acknowledging the complexity of reform, said the difficulty goes beyond partisan politics.

“It’s not like there’s a clear fix for all of this stuff,” she said, adding that “we’ve stopped even talking about it because it just seems such a remote possibility that it’ll happen.”

**

Cazares’ story is hardly an outlier. It is more the norm. Walter Pascual said he tried for years to obtain legal status after he entered the country in 2005 from Guatemala.

He learned he first needed to be arrested and detained.

“Literally, there’s no way” otherwise, he said.

“All the people who have been here 20 years, 30 years, and who have never had contact with immigration, if they don’t have children, if they don’t have anything, if they haven’t married a citizen, there is no way.”

Pascual has gained a following on social media for documenting immigration enforcement in and around Chicago. He was working as a driver last October, on his way to a pickup at a hotel, when he was arrested. He can remember what one of the federal agents told him:

“Welcome, Walter. We’ve been waiting for you.”

Pascual, 37, spent almost three months in detention. He’ll spend years in uncertainty before he knows if he can remain in the country. For the first time, though, he has a work permit, which offers some level of protection while his case continues. He said he’s not scared — “I have a little bit of concern, but not fear” — but he may well be an anomaly that way.

In another part of Chicago, a 48-year-old man named Jose — who only wanted to be identified by his first name — remains afraid to leave home. He spent 76 days in federal custody. Agents apprehended him early last October, when he’d been working his landscaping job, cutting grass.

He wound up in Broadview. Then in a jail in Missouri. He paid a $10,000 bond to be released, but only after his sister gave him half and his three children and neighbors raised the rest. And he now must raise more money to pay the attorney working his case. He is at home now but not free.

He has no criminal record. Three American-born children.

“If I have to leave, what are they going to do?” he asked of his family.

There’s nothing for him to do but wait and hope. In the aftermath of detainment, the released carry burdens that manifest in a variety of trauma responses, said Lu Rocha, a Chicago therapist.

“Anxiety, panic attacks, hypervigilance, very easily startled, flashbacks, insomnia, inability to fall asleep for fear of dreaming about the traumatic events,” she said.

Jose hesitates to go to McDonald’s. What if ICE approaches him while he’s there?

Inside the Missouri jail, he was surrounded by those also facing deportation. He said about 50 people from the Chicago area were transported there at the same time he was. Eventually, only about 10 remained. Some were deported. Others were released on bonds that varied widely.

One person paid $5,000. Another paid $7,500. Someone else paid $20,000. Jose’s was $10,000.

He’s still trying to pay back those who raised the money. He’s still waiting for his work authorization, and his next court date. And he is still trying to understand what release ultimately means. Jose keeps the same paperwork that an ICE agent handed Freddy Cazares. They treat the documents like amulets, as if they have the power to keep them safe.

Immediately after their release, they experienced the obvious range of emotions. But now there’s the lingering unknown amid a fight that can feel endless.

“I came here to work and pay taxes,” Cazares said. “I’m not a bad person.”

His August appointment at The Resurrection Project represented one more step in a long journey. He walked downstairs when it ended and the clouds of a rainy morning were starting to break. There was plenty of daylight left and Cazares decided to do what he’d done most days since arriving in America 22 years ago: He set out to go work.

title: Attorney says too many mothers arrested amid ICE crackdown | Opinion
description:
I was sworn in as an attorney to the Tennessee Bar almost 19 years ago, and I became a mother less than two years later.
Single moms, pregnant moms, nursing moms, moms of children with special needs and moms of ordinary children who love and depend on them, as children ordinarily do.
Calls like this now come daily, and increasingly from the family and friends of mothers ripped from their children.
In fact, the majority of those arrested by ICE in Tennessee navigate the detention and removal process without an attorney.
There are an estimated 70,000 children in Tennessee at risk of being separated from a parent by ICE.
text:
I was sworn in as an attorney to the Tennessee Bar almost 19 years ago, and I became a mother less than two years later. I could never have imagined then what I am experiencing now: that my work requires me to bear daily witness to state cruelty towards mothers and children that I am too often powerless to stop.

For the last year and a half, I have been on the front lines of a human rights crisis unfolding in plain sight. The Trump administration has aggressively imposed a brutal campaign of mass detention and deportation, sparing no one. In recent months, an inordinate number of those caught in the crosshairs of this campaign are mothers. Single moms, pregnant moms, nursing moms, moms of children with special needs and moms of ordinary children who love and depend on them, as children ordinarily do.

As a mom of two daughters, I am hurt. As an attorney, I am exhausted. And as a human being, I am fed up.

The terror of ICE

I still remember the call a few months into the second Trump administration that signaled unprecedented, terrifying new times. We learned of an elderly landscaper who had been taken from the street by masked, plainclothed officers in unmarked SUVs. The only charges against him were alleged violations of civil immigration law, which is by its very definition not a crime. Yet within hours he was in ICE custody on the other side of the state and quickly shipped to a detention center hundreds of miles away from his family and home.

Since he wasn’t accused of a crime, he had no guaranteed right to an attorney, no right to a fast, fair hearing before a judge, no protection from being transported across state lines by government agents. His decades of living, working and paying taxes in the U.S. meant nothing in the face of an administration that has continually trampled on the norms of our legal system in order to carry out a racial restructuring of our country through mass detention and deportation.

Calls like this now come daily, and increasingly from the family and friends of mothers ripped from their children. The callers are desperate for the legal help it takes to bring those mothers home.

The children separated from their mothers

On the same day ICE released one of my clients who was still nursing her infant daughter and toddler with Down Syndrome when she was detained, I received requests for help from two other single mothers detained in Middle Tennessee. One was a single mom of a child with special needs; another was a mom of teenagers left to fend for themselves for months while their mother languishes in detention in Louisiana.

Their stories spun through my head alongside the knowledge that 145,000 U.S. citizen children have had a parent detained or deported: the working mom detained by ICE after dropping off an infant and toddler at day care; the mom of three who came to the U.S. many years ago, arrested at a courthouse when she went to pay a traffic ticket; the many other single mothers whose arrests forced older children to become caregivers to younger siblings.

I can’t stop thinking about those children, infants abruptly cut off from their mother’s milk, children navigating the first days of the school year without the comfort of a mother’s hugs, teenagers bravely trying to reassure their mothers through phone calls that they are holding up on their own.

We must shine a light, and speak out

Some of these moms have lived in the U.S. for decades, working, paying taxes, raising their families. Some arrived more recently, fleeing violence and upheaval in their home countries in the hopes of finding safety here. None of them have been charged with any crime more serious than driving without a license, and most landed in ICE custody through traffic stops or routine appointments as part of their immigration processes.

Being represented by a competent attorney is practically a necessity for anyone hoping to escape the claws of this mass detention and deportation regime, but without a right to counsel in immigration proceedings, detained moms must turn to a patchwork of private attorneys and scarce nonprofit legal resources as they confront the singular nightmare of being separated from their children. In fact, the majority of those arrested by ICE in Tennessee navigate the detention and removal process without an attorney.

There are an estimated 70,000 children in Tennessee at risk of being separated from a parent by ICE. Tennessee certainly needs more high quality, affordable immigration legal resources, because attorneys are the last line of defense in this human rights crisis brought about by our government. But more lawyers alone will not get us out of this nightmare.

It’s the responsibility of those of us on the front lines of the crisis to shine a light on it. And more importantly, it is the responsibility of all of us Tennesseans to to say, “Not in our name.”

So while it is in my work as a lawyer that I have had a front-row view to these stories, it is as a human and a mother that I am compelled to speak out.

ICE must stop. Not in my name.

Spring Miler is the Senior Director of Legal Strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC) with more than two decades of experience in immigrants' rights advocacy in legal and community-based settings. Prior to joining TIRRC in 2023, she spent nine years at Vanderbilt Law School as assistant dean for public interest and a lecturer in law, teaching experiential courses on immigrant and worker rights and overseeing the law school’s public interest program.

text:
HENRICO COUNTY, Va. (WRIC) — Protesters lined up outside Richmond International Airport (RIC) Saturday morning demanding a stop to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) flights at their local airfield.

So far this year, 128 detainee flights have passed through Richmond, according to ICE Flight Tracker, which is run by a human rights organization.

“I don’t think that Richmonders are going to be happy with knowing our airport is being used to shuffle detainees from place to place,” said Paul Fleisher, one of the event organizers and a member of RVA Indivisible.

Fleisher said he first noticed planes with names like “GlobalX” this spring. According to the non-profit Open Secrets, which cites an immigration activist, GlobalX is one of the largest subcontractors used by ICE.

Fleisher started organizing this protest when he realized what was happening. Fleisher and another protester told 8News they also saw unmarked buses near the non-commercial planes.

“It’s un-American,” said Deborah Brown, who was in attendance with her husband, an RVA Indivisible member. “It’s not loving your neighbor as yourself. It’s full of hate, and I don’t want this for my grandchildren.”

The flights coming through RIC are described as “shuffle flights.” This means detainees are being transferred between US detention centers, not internationally.

When asked about the protest, the Capital Region Airport Commission gave 8News the following statement:

As a public-use airport, RIC cannot prohibit flights that are legally authorized. The Capital Region Airport Commission, which operates the airport, does not schedule, direct, handle, or make operational decisions regarding these federal flights. The Commission’s role is to maintain a safe, secure, and operational airport. We respect the right to peaceful expression and assembly under the law. Questions about the purpose or conduct of these flights should be directed to the responsible federal agency.

“We’re all immigrants, and we’re all human beings, and they’re treating people this way, and this is not who we are,” said Robin Barber, an RVA Indivisible member.

title: Big bucks made off human misery - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
authors: ROD LORENZEN Special to the Democrat-Gazette
description:
The United States now operates the world's largest immigration detention system, with more than 200 facilities: detention centers, jails and prisons.
That means private prison operators are making big bucks off their cozy working relationship with the government.
Many constitutional protections available under criminal law don't exist in the civil detention system.
Critics believe the administration is buying private detention centers to clamp down on any oversight and could possibly use them for other nefarious purposes.
According to the results of the study, the ICE detention program is guilty on all four counts.
text:
Business is booming for the private prison business, thanks in large part to an administration that has ushered cruelty into fashion and also provided plenty of new growth opportunities.

The two biggest contractors for building and managing detention centers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) posted record revenue in 2025 and are expanding their facilities nationwide to hold more immigrants apprehended by the Trump administration.

The United States now operates the world's largest immigration detention system, with more than 200 facilities: detention centers, jails and prisons. That means private prison operators are making big bucks off their cozy working relationship with the government. Here's how a recent article in a national magazine broke it down: "The largest immigration deportation and prison camp contractors in the U.S. are expecting an epic payout this year. For every $1 that they donated to GOP campaigns in 2024, these private companies stand to reap more than $11,000 in increased annual revenue."

GEO Group, which now has over $2 billion in ICE contracts and operates 19 facilities for ICE around the country, reported $2.6 billion in total revenue in 2025, up 6 percent from $2.34 billion in 2024. CoreCivic, which owns and operates at least 10 ICE facilities, reported $2.2 billion in total revenue in 2025, up 13 percent from $1.96 billion in 2024.

Sometimes it's hard to see much separation between the government and these private businesses. Last May, Trump picked a former GEO Group executive, David Venturella, to be the acting head of ICE. Trump's border czar Tom Homan was a paid consultant for GEO before joining the government, and Pam Bondi lobbied for GEO before she was appointed attorney general.

Maybe it's mere coincidence that, according to a Washington watchdog, Trump and his brokers have made 29 trades of private prison stocks since he returned to office. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) says Trump traded these stocks every month of 2025 with the exception of August and December. The total amount of stock bought and sold was between $281,029 and $990,000, split between the two companies that have benefited massively from Trump administration policy--GEO Group and CoreCivic.

Software giant Palantir Technologies (PLTR), which works with ICE, is also cashing in. Palantir recently won a $30 million contract from ICE to develop a system that identifies undocumented immigrants and tracks self-deportations. The American Civil Liberties Union claims the company is building applications that are customized to the Trump administration's questionable goals and tactics, which include mass removal without due process, random identity checks and racial profiling.

Palantir, which also developed an app that can be used to hack into your phone, expects revenue between $7.18 billion and $7.2 billion this year, which would be more than a 60 percent increase from 2025. Its founder, Peter Thiel, was an early backer of Trump and has close ties with key Washington lawmakers, including vice president JD Vance, whom he supported in a 2022 Senate race.

During the first three months of the year, Trump purchased between $247,008 and $630,000 worth of stock in Miami-based Palantir, according to CNBC. In March alone, Trump made at least seven purchases of Palantir stock totaling as much as $530,000. A month later, as Palantir shares were having their worst week in over a year, Trump gave the company a generous shout-out on his social media platform Truth Social.

Now, amid its explosive growth, comes news that Palantir has paid zero taxes on its huge profits over the last three years. Last year, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economics Policy, the company's increased income was $1.5 billion yet it avoided taxes, thanks to handouts from American taxpayers.

ITEP says we are paying multiple times for the services provided by Palantir. First, we pay the bill for government contracts with Palantir, then we pay again through government subsidies for Palantir.

Trump's so-called Big Beautiful Bill now allows companies to (retroactively) immediately deduct their research expenses rather than writing them off over time in line with the income generated from that research. Using this method, Palantir reduced its taxes by over $400 million and skipped out on paying any federal income tax.

But as these companies line their pockets, there are serious side effects to consider. The immigration detention system, unlike criminal jails or prisons, operates under civil law. Many constitutional protections available under criminal law don't exist in the civil detention system.

For example, immigrants can be detained indefinitely under harsh conditions. There is no federal right to legal representation for detainees and most immigrants are not entitled to government-appointed lawyers, greatly reducing their chances of winning their cases. They are often held in conditions so miserable that they will choose to "self-deport' rather than stick it out to pursue legal remedies.

While the stated goal of ICE is to sweep up immigrants with criminal records, as of April of this year numerous sources say that more than 70 percent of those arrested have no criminal record and many are being held only for minor traffic violations. The Detention Watch Network, a coalition of Christian organizations, says ICE's dragnet approach to making arrests in order to meet its quotas is appalling and that 31 people died in ICE custody last year.

"The U.S. locks up survivors of torture, people seeking asylum, visa holders, people who have been granted the right to live in the U.S., people who have lived here for decades and may have American citizen spouses and children, individuals with mental health and medical conditions and other vulnerable groups. The government also jails parents with their children."

Claire Trickler-McNally, a former senior ICE official, said one of the reasons so many problems persist at ICE detention centers is the reduction of oversight from internal watchdog offices. The Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, created by Congress in 2020 to investigate facilities that fall short of detention standards, and the Office for Civil Rights and Liberties, which protects the civil rights of detained immigrants, were both dismantled by former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem.

The civil deportation process, Trickler-McNally said, doesn't have to be as aggressive and violent toward individuals as it is right now, since the majority of detained immigrants have no criminal record."I see way more 'Abolish ICE' signs now than I saw before," she told Time magazine. "People are mad, and this is all just a choice of how to enforce immigration law. It really doesn't have to be this way."

Over the summer, the U.S. government quietly began buying its own detention centers from the CoreCivic group. ICE paid $739.2 million for the Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego and $732.6 for the California City Detention Facility in Kern County. ICE also bought the Prairie Correctional Facility in Minnesota and the Midwest Regional Reception Center in Kansas for a total of $734 million.

Critics believe the administration is buying private detention centers to clamp down on any oversight and could possibly use them for other nefarious purposes. A spokesman for the American Immigration Council said that "once the facility is entirely owned by the federal government, that limits the ability of state and local inspectors to try to gain some insight about what is happening in there, or seek changes to conditions that may be potentially violative of people's rights."

The growth and maintenance of such facilities "normalizes" civil incarceration and portends a darker future for democracy at large, where the government may try to jail people other than immigrants such as journalists, dissenters and political enemies.

Researchers Alex Braithwaite from the University of Arizona and Rachel D. Van Nostrand from Louisiana State University recently shared the results of their work in looking at 150 historical cases involving the use of concentration camps throughout the world since the late 1800s.

The study included the U.S. internment of more than 125,000 Japanese immigrants and Japanese American citizens during World War II, the Argentine military junta's use of camps in their mid-1970s campaign to reorganize society, Vladimir Putin's use of so-called filtration camps in Russia's war against Ukraine, and concentration camps in China.

"Our use of the term 'concentration camp' is not meant to sensationalize or diminish its historical meaning, particularly as it relates to the Holocaust," the researchers explained.

"Rather, identifying such systems early is how the concept of 'never again'--the promise to prevent mass atrocities, such as genocide, and combat extremism--can be translated into meaningful policy action from the public and policymakers."

They identified four characteristics that define what qualifies as a concentration camp: Targeting groups of civilians for imprisonment; enclosed spaces where the state controls who enters and exits; departure from standard detention practices; and abuse and neglect of detainees.

According to the results of the study, the ICE detention program is guilty on all four counts.

Rod Lorenzen is a writer who lives in Little Rock.

text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R-Texas) announced Friday that a Houston-area “birth tourism” center accused of helping Chinese nationals travel to Texas to give birth and obtain U.S. citizenship for their children has agreed to close.

De’Ai Postpartum Care Center and its operators agreed to cease operations under a proposed final judgment and permanent injunction filed September 18 in Fort Bend County District Court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Paxton’s office described the resolution as a legal victory and said the center will stop facilitating births and coaching foreign nationals on how to evade immigration restrictions.

As previously reported by The Dallas Express, Paxton sued the center in April, alleging that it primarily marketed services to Chinese clients and had claimed responsibility for “1,000+ American-born babies.”

The state also alleged the operation used at least four Houston-area properties and coached clients on U.S. visa procedures, including advising women to apply for visas “before pregnancy” to reduce scrutiny.

“I will do everything in my power to stop foreign nationals from unlawfully exploiting our immigration system through the scam of ‘birth tourism,’” Paxton said. “This operation helped Chinese foreign nationals come to Texas to evade our laws. Now, we have shut it down.”

State Case Focused On Alleged Visa And Consumer-Law Violations

The State Department states that travel for the primary purpose of giving birth in the United States to obtain U.S. citizenship for a child is not a permissible basis for a visitor visa. Paxton’s civil petition accused De’Ai and operators Lin Suling and Lai Wan Lin-Chan of deceptive trade practices, tampering with governmental records, unlawful harboring and concealment, and other alleged violations of Texas law.

The operators had denied the state’s allegations in court filings before the proposed injunction, reported Texas Public Radio.

Birthright Citizenship Remains Unchanged

The U.S. Supreme Court held June 30 in Trump v. Barbara that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Texas case targeted the center’s alleged business and immigration-related conduct.

Nothing in the proposed Texas judgment purports to revoke citizenship from children previously born to the center’s clients.”

title: Federal Judge Blocks DHS Student Visa Policy - Chicago Maroon
description:
A federal judge on Monday temporarily blocked a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy implementing new, more restrictive rules on how long students on F and J visas can stay in the United States without renewing their status.
International students would have also been prevented from seeking multiple degrees at the same level of study.
International student enrollment in the U.S. had already been declining since President Donald Trump began his second term.
At the time of publication, DHS had not filed an appeal.
DHS did not respond to questions about whether it planned to submit one but criticized the “performative outrage” of the media in a statement to the Maroon.
text:
A federal judge on Monday temporarily blocked a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy implementing new, more restrictive rules on how long students on F and J visas can stay in the United States without renewing their status.

In his ruling, District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV said that the government had provided little evidence for how it would accommodate the new rules and had failed to reasonably justify them, and that DHS’s current plan for enforcement would be “entirely discretionary and unappealable.”

The policy, which was set to go into effect the following day, would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” (D/S) model for student visa holders with an “admit until date” (AUD), requiring students to reapply for authorization after four years, regardless of whether they had completed their program.

The new rules also would have prevented undergraduates from transferring institutions or programs of study during their first year and graduate students from doing so at any point. International students would have also been prevented from seeking multiple degrees at the same level of study.

Under Saylor’s September 14 ruling, the government is “preliminarily enjoined from taking any further action to implement the Final Rule,” and students who entered the U.S. after September 15 will retain D/S until the end of their enrollment in an academic program. The ruling remains in place until the court has a chance to hear arguments from both parties about whether the policy should be allowed to go into effect.

In an email to international students on Monday, the University’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) wrote that it would “continue to follow this issue closely” and would “share information and updates as they become available.” It also advised students to reach out to their OIA advisors with questions.

The Association of American Universities and the Association of American Medical Colleges, of which the University of Chicago and the Pritzker School of Medicine are members, respectively, filed a joint amicus brief—a document submitted by those who are not party to the case but have a stake in its outcome—in support of the plaintiffs, eight education and labor organizations including the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration and the American Federation of Teachers.

Saylor found that the government had failed to meet its responsibilities under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires that agency action “‘be reasonable and reasonably explained’ and the agency must ‘examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.’”

“The rule contains limited guidance, at best, for the exercise of discretion by DHS in considering such a request,” Saylor wrote. “The government has provided no indication as to how the immigration system will be expanded, or funded, to accommodate a large influx of such requests.” In its analysis, DHS said that the new visa restrictions could cost more than $400 million annually in fees and administrative costs to students and institutions.

Saylor also cited a 2025 survey conducted by one of the plaintiffs that found that 49 percent of current international students would not have enrolled in a U.S. school under the AUD model. International student enrollment in the U.S. had already been declining since President Donald Trump began his second term.

“DHS dispensed with the studies simply by saying that survey data was unreliable,” Saylor wrote, responding “only that it ‘acknowledge[d] that enrollment of foreign students in U.S. educational institutions may decline,’ and that it was impossible to ‘quantify the extent of this decline’ because of lack of ‘precedent from which accurate conclusions [could] be drawn as to the rule’s impact.’”

According to Saylor, DHS’s outright dismissal of potential costs to enrollment meant that it failed to comply with the APA’s requirements that rulemaking not be “arbitrary and capricious,” and that agencies make a good faith effort to weigh the costs and benefits of new rules.

At the time of publication, DHS had not filed an appeal. DHS did not respond to questions about whether it planned to submit one but criticized the “performative outrage” of the media in a statement to the Maroon.

BROADVIEW, Ill. (WLS) -- Federal officers used pepper spray against protesters Saturday during a clash outside the Broadview U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility after demonstrators blocked the facility's driveway as officers attempted to enter and leave, according to video of the incident.

Video shows demonstrators gathered at the gate and blocking the driveway as federal officers attempted to drive through. Some protesters can be seen holding on to the hood of a vehicle as officers drove through the crowd.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

The Coalition Against Broadview ICE Facility, a group involved in the demonstration, called for an independent federal investigation into the incident and raised concerns about the use of force against protesters.

"Peaceful protesters should never be subjected to unnecessary force or actions that place their safety at risk," the coalition said in a statement.

Robert Held, an attorney with the Chicago Council of Lawyers who said he was at the demonstration during the escalation, criticized the officers' response.

"It's just shocking. It's disappointing," Held said.

Held said federal agents repeatedly emerged from the facility to move protesters away from the driveway.

"ICE would open the gate to their parking lot, and dozens of agents would march out aggressively. They were pushing people away from the driveway, but they were doing it in an aggressive and violent manner," Held said.

Video from the scene also captures Held questioning a masked federal officer about the agents' response.

"One question, when you come out, why do you escalate when you come out?" Held asked.

The masked officer said protesters had repeatedly been told to stay out of the driveway.

"We've asked them multiple times to stay out of the driveway. It's very simple. The request is very simple. I've tried my best to be very request, so I hate that she had to get sprayed, but this has been going on for an elongated period of time," the officer said.

In its statement, the coalition said several demonstrators were exposed to pepper spray. The group also alleged that an ICE vehicle made contact with a protester and that a seated protester was forcibly removed despite posing no apparent threat.

The coalition disputed portions of public statements attributed to City of Broadview spokesperson David Ormsby regarding the confrontation, saying those statements did not fully account for actions taken against protesters and omitted details about the conduct of federal agents.

"We believe the public deserves a complete and accurate account of what occurred during this demonstration. Peaceful protesters should never be subjected to unnecessary force or actions that place their safety at risk. We are particularly concerned by reports that pepper spray was used against demonstrators, that an ICE vehicle struck a protester, and that a seated individual was physically removed despite presenting no threat. We call for an independent federal investigation into these incidents and for full transparency regarding the actions of all parties involved," the coalition said.

The coalition also called on federal authorities, elected officials and independent oversight bodies to review available video, eyewitness accounts and incident reports.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security was contacted for comment about the clash but has not yet responded.

Mental health advocates say the heightened concern is affecting immigrant and refugee communities across North Carolina.

text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- More than 5,000 people have been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in North Carolina so far this year, according to data from the Deportation Data Project analyzed by the ABC News Data Team.

The data shows ICE detained more than 253,000 people nationwide this year. In North Carolina alone, ICE apprehended more than 5,000 people, including at least 441 arrests in the Raleigh area.

Immigration advocates and attorneys in the Triangle say increased enforcement activity is contributing to fear and anxiety among immigrants and their families.

"We're definitely seeing increased activity with this," said Trey DeBrine, an immigration law attorney with Sivaraman Immigration Law.

The concerns come months after Operation Charlotte's Web, an immigration enforcement operation that brought a surge of activity by immigration agents in the Triangle in November. Advocates say continued arrests have left many people fearful of carrying out everyday activities.

"People with status are afraid to do things like drive, because they think, 'I'm gonna get pulled over, I'm gonna get arrested, and I'm gonna get put into ICE custody,'" DeBrine said.

DeBrine also said his office has heard of people being detained during routine immigration appointments.

"What we're seeing now is people who are getting detained at regular check-ins," he said.

According to the data, about 28% of people detained nationwide this year were convicted criminals, 30% had pending criminal charges and more than 40% had no criminal history.

Mental health advocates say the heightened concern is affecting immigrant and refugee communities across North Carolina.

"Because of this fear, it's having an effect overall in the quality of life of North Carolinians," said Molly Hayes, head of learning and dissemination at El Futuro.

Hayes said fear and uncertainty can create additional barriers to obtaining mental health care.

"The stress, the fear, the anxiety, the stigma, the things that really have prevented folks from getting the mental health care that they need have, have become more challenging," Hayes said.

The concerns coincide with the release of El Futuro's Immigrant Mental Health Solidarity Report, which highlights mental health needs within immigrant and refugee communities through a collaborative analysis with other organizations. The report emphasizes reducing barriers to care by meeting people where they are.

"Reimbursing services such as home visiting and community health worker visits, supporting training for community health workers and peer support specialists that really highlight the particular needs of immigrant and refugee communities," Hayes said.

text:
(NEW YORK) — A federal appeals court ruled Friday that immigrants facing deportation to third countries must be given sufficient notice before being sent to nations where they have no ties.

The unanimous decision by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit struck down a Department of Homeland Security policy that allowed the swift deportation of immigrants to third countries.

“An individual’s right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” wrote Circuit Judge Seth Aframe.

The ruling on Friday allows migrants to contest deportations to countries other than their place of origin.

According to the lawsuit, immigrants were routinely transferred to third countries with little to no notice when the administration cited “diplomatic assurances” that the receiving nation would not mistreat them.

ABC News previously interviewed a group of Latin American men who were deported to the Central African Republic and were not informed of their destination until several hours into the flight.

“I feel kidnapped,” one of the men, Aristides Fernandez Garcia, said. “They have violated all the rights that exist in life, because we are human beings.”

In recent months, the administration has expanded third-country deportations after securing formal deals with 35 countries, including Liberia, Ghana, the Central African Republic and Sierra Leone.

Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said the U.S. has spent nearly $50 million on these deportation agreements.

“I think the fact that the administration is sending refugees to the most dangerous countries in the world, to countries run by corrupt autocrats where they’ve been arbitrarily detained and sent back to persecution and torture, shows that the administration has a complete disregard for due process, for international law and for human dignity,” Arvey said.

title: By fixating on immigration numbers, are our leaders missing the bigger picture for working ...
description:
But, in fact, Burke’s address was a message for all working people across the country – and a signal of the times ahead for all of us.
In fact, judging by the tenor of current debate, it would be easy to think that immigration is the only economic lever available to the government to address housing affordability, falling wages and cost-of-living pressures.
There is an attractively simple supply-and-demand logic underlying the assumption that fewer people will automatically mean more to go around.
But as long as public debate remains fixated on immigration numbers, the bigger policy questions that could actually transform the lives of working people will remain unanswered.
For decades, governments have re-geared the migration system towards temporary migration and shifted the goalposts on permanent residency.
text:
When the immigration minister, Tony Burke, approached the National Press Club podium on Thursday, the eyes of every migrant in the country would have been fixed on him. But, in fact, Burke’s address was a message for all working people across the country – and a signal of the times ahead for all of us.

The past 12 months have seen all sides of politics cohere around the consensus articulated in the introduction to Burke’s address by the press club’s president, Tom Connell: “there is furious agreement over a need for a cut to immigration.” The only difference across the political spectrum is in the detail: who deserves to be cut, and who is valuable or otherwise deserving enough to remain.

In fact, judging by the tenor of current debate, it would be easy to think that immigration is the only economic lever available to the government to address housing affordability, falling wages and cost-of-living pressures. To test that theory, consider whether, over a Sunday lunch, your uncle is more likely to proffer an opinion on tax settings driving housing speculation, the corporate supermarket duopoly or immigration levels? There is an attractively simple supply-and-demand logic underlying the assumption that fewer people will automatically mean more to go around.

But migrants didn’t design – and then implement over 20 years – the tax breaks that transformed housing into an asset, allowing investors to drive up prices and control distribution through property hoarding. And it wasn’t migrants, sitting in state and federal legislatures, who chose to wind back investment in public housing that previous generations had benefited from.

Migrants didn’t mastermind the attacks on collective bargaining that have seen union membership and real wages plummet over the past two decades. And they didn’t invent the supermarket duopoly or dictate the eye-watering profits that Coles and Woolworths maintain, driving up grocery prices while wages remain stagnant.

But as long as public debate remains fixated on immigration numbers, the bigger policy questions that could actually transform the lives of working people will remain unanswered. And there will be an endless, self-fulfilling cycle of blame targeting our friends, neighbours and co-workers born overseas for problems not of their making.

Burke set the scene for future blame-shifting. Design features of our migration program are ascribed to temporary migrants as a kind of collective moral failing. For decades, governments have re-geared the migration system towards temporary migration and shifted the goalposts on permanent residency. The natural result of this – that people transition between temporary visas to realise their hopes of permanent migration – has been recast as an illegitimate form of “visa-hopping”.

International students and graduates will no longer be able to migrate with their partners and children because, according to Burke, they should not receive special treatment compared with permanent residents and citizens forced to wait years for family reunion. But family visa processing blowouts are the direct result of ministerial directions that deprioritise and slow down some applications.

The path has been cleared for more “comprehensive” measures to come, when political and economic pressures demand them. The government has repeatedly floated the idea of legislating a 30-day window on asylum applications, requiring new migrants to make a claim immediately or miss out. This would, of course, force people seeking asylum who have missed the eligibility window to remain in the community without a visa, exposing them either to destitution, exploitative work in the cash economy or being rounded up in immigration raids.

As tempting as it might be to blame grievance politics, far-right organising or the electoral rise of One Nation for the current impasse, these are just symptoms of a much deeper malaise. It will always be in the interests of our political leaders and their backers to deflect blame for economic conditions away from themselves and on to people who cannot speak back at the ballot box.

By continuing to allow immigration to be the scapegoat for economic grievance, we not only abandon refugees and migrants to endless cycles of blame – we abandon working people to the very conditions that produced the grievances in the first place.

Introduction

In Davison v. Bisignano (10th Cir. Sept. 17, 2026), Daniel Joseph Davison, proceeding pro se, appealed the District of Colorado’s dismissal of his amended complaint against the Social Security Administration (SSA), the Commissioner, and the United States. Mr. Davison alleged he was seriously injured in 2006 and claimed he was entitled to substantial retroactive Social Security Disability Insurance benefits for a “Childhood Disability” dating back to 2006, alleging the SSA owed him $165,796 in retroactive pay.

He attempted to proceed in federal district court by invoking diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 and asserted claims styled as Federal Tort Claims Act claims and a breach of contract claim. The central jurisdictional question was whether the district court could hear the dispute outside the Social Security Act’s judicial review provision, 42 U.S.C. § 405(g), and whether Mr. Davison properly alleged (and later adequately briefed on appeal) the facts necessary to invoke that limited jurisdiction.

Summary of the Opinion

The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The court agreed that:

Diversity jurisdiction was unavailable because the United States is not a citizen for diversity purposes and federal agencies/administrators cannot be sued in diversity.

Federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 was unavailable because § 405(g) is the exclusive route for judicial review of claims arising under the Social Security Act, and Mr. Davison’s amended complaint did not allege administrative exhaustion necessary to invoke § 405(g).

Assertions in objections to the magistrate judge’s recommendation that he completed the administrative process could not substitute for allegations missing from the operative amended complaint.

On appeal, Mr. Davison’s briefing did not meaningfully engage the district court’s jurisdictional reasoning; inadequately developed arguments were treated as waived.

Analysis

Precedents Cited

1. James v. Wadas, 724 F.3d 1312 (10th Cir. 2013)

The panel cited James v. Wadas for the familiar rule that courts liberally construe pro se filings but do not serve as the litigant’s advocate. This principle framed the opinion’s approach: Mr. Davison received liberal construction, but the court still required him to satisfy jurisdictional pleading requirements and appellate briefing rules.

2. Smith v. Berryhill, 587 U.S. 471 (2019)

The court relied on Smith v. Berryhill to describe the “modern-day” four-step administrative process generally required before judicial review: (1) initial determination, (2) reconsideration, (3) ALJ hearing, (4) Appeals Council review. The case supplied the doctrinal content of “administrative exhaustion” in Social Security litigation and underscored why a complaint must plausibly allege completion of these steps (or some legally recognized basis to excuse them) to invoke § 405(g).

3. Heckler v. Ringer, 466 U.S. 602 (1984)

The magistrate judge (and district court) invoked Heckler v. Ringer for the key jurisdictional proposition that § 405(g), to the exclusion of 28 U.S.C. § 1331, is the sole avenue for judicial review for all claims arising under the Social Security Act. This precedent is the backbone of the decision: even if a plaintiff labels claims as tort or contract theories, the court looks to substance—if the claim is in essence about entitlement to benefits or the agency’s benefits decision, the Social Security Act channels review through § 405(g).

4. Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer, 425 F.3d 836 (10th Cir. 2005)

The panel cited Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer for two related points: (1) pro se litigants must follow the same procedural rules as other litigants, and (2) appellate briefs must do more than assert generalized error; they must provide developed argument with supporting authority. This authority directly supported the holding that Mr. Davison’s appellate presentation was inadequate to secure review of the district court’s dismissal.

5. United States v. Pinson, 584 F.3d 972 (10th Cir. 2009)

United States v. Pinson reinforced the boundary of liberal construction: it “stops” when the court would be forced to act as an advocate. In practical terms, the court would not craft jurisdictional arguments or reconstruct a compliant pleading or appellate brief for Mr. Davison.

6. Adams v. Fed. Aviation Admin., 168 F.4th 1271 (10th Cir. 2026)

The panel relied on Adams v. Fed. Aviation Admin. for the rule that arguments inadequately briefed in the opening brief are waived. This provided the decisive appellate mechanism: even if an appellant believes the district court erred, failure to develop a reasoned challenge to the dispositive grounds for dismissal typically ends the appeal.

7. Ohlsen v. United States, 998 F.3d 1143 (10th Cir. 2021)

The court cited Ohlsen v. United States to decline review of Mr. Davison’s recusal claim. Because he did not move for recusal in the district court and only indirectly mentioned it in objections (while withholding his asserted basis), the issue was not adequately presented below; consistent with Ohlsen, the panel declined to consider it for the first time on appeal.

Legal Reasoning

No diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332. The operative defendants were federal: the SSA, the Commissioner, and the United States. Diversity jurisdiction requires “citizens” of different states; the United States is not a state citizen for diversity purposes, and federal agencies/officers sued in their official capacities do not create diversity. This foreclosed the jurisdictional basis Mr. Davison invoked.

§ 405(g) is the exclusive channel for benefits-related claims. Under Heckler v. Ringer, claims “arising under” the Social Security Act must proceed through § 405(g). Mr. Davison’s requested relief—retroactive disability benefits and alleged underpayment—squarely implicated the Act’s benefits adjudication scheme, regardless of his choice to plead tort and contract labels.

Failure to plead exhaustion in the amended complaint defeats § 405(g) jurisdiction. The district court required allegations showing completion of the administrative steps described in Smith v. Berryhill. Mr. Davison insisted (in objections) that he completed them, but his amended complaint did not allege such facts. Because subject matter jurisdiction must be established on the operative pleadings and the plaintiff bears the burden of demonstrating it, the absence of exhaustion allegations supported dismissal under Rule 12(b)(1).

Objections to a recommendation are not a proper vehicle to amend the operative complaint. The district court treated Mr. Davison’s attempt to add exhaustion facts through objections as procedurally improper. The Tenth Circuit did not disturb that conclusion; instead, it noted Mr. Davison did not meaningfully challenge this reasoning on appeal.

Inadequate appellate briefing results in waiver. Applying Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer and Adams v. Fed. Aviation Admin., the panel held that generalized assertions that the magistrate judge and government were “wrong,” coupled with failure to engage the district court’s specific jurisdictional grounds, amounted to inadequate briefing. With no developed argument demonstrating reversible error, the court declined substantive review and affirmed.

Recusal issue not preserved. Under Ohlsen v. United States, the recusal claim was forfeited because it was not properly raised in the district court by motion, and the panel found no compelling reason to address it for the first time on appeal.

Impact

Although the decision is designated as a nonprecedential “Order and Judgment,” it is significant for its practical, recurring lessons in Social Security litigation—especially for pro se claimants:

Pleading discipline in § 405(g) cases: Claimants must allege (not merely believe or later assert) facts showing completion of the administrative process—or otherwise explain a legally cognizable basis for jurisdiction. Courts will not infer exhaustion when the complaint is silent.

Channeling and re-labeling: Attempting to repackage benefits disputes as FTCA or contract claims is unlikely to avoid the Social Security Act’s exclusive review route under Heckler v. Ringer.

Procedure matters as much as substance: Even if a claimant could ultimately show exhaustion, failing to place the necessary allegations in the operative complaint can lead to dismissal—though here, importantly, without prejudice, preserving the possibility of refiling with proper jurisdictional allegations.

Appellate briefing as a gatekeeper: The opinion underscores that appellate courts will affirm when appellants do not confront the district court’s dispositive reasoning with developed argument and authority, even when filings are liberally construed.

Complex Concepts Simplified

Subject matter jurisdiction

The court’s legal power to hear a particular type of dispute. If jurisdiction is missing, the case must be dismissed even if the plaintiff might otherwise have a valid grievance.

Diversity jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1332)

A basis for federal jurisdiction when opposing parties are citizens of different states and the amount in controversy is met. The United States and its agencies are not “citizens” for diversity purposes.

Federal question jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1331) vs. § 405(g)

Federal question jurisdiction is broad, but in Social Security benefits disputes Congress provided a specific, limited pathway—42 U.S.C. § 405(g)—that generally displaces § 1331 for claims “arising under” the Act.

Administrative exhaustion (the four-step process)

Before a federal court can review a benefits dispute, claimants usually must pursue the agency process through an initial determination, reconsideration, an ALJ hearing, and Appeals Council review. Completion of these steps is what typically generates a reviewable “final decision.”

Rule 12(b)(1) dismissal

A motion arguing the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction. Such dismissals are commonly without prejudice because the court is not reaching the merits.

Waiver for inadequate briefing

On appeal, courts generally consider only issues that are clearly argued, supported by reasoning, and (typically) supported by legal authority. A bare assertion that the lower court was wrong is usually not enough.

Issue preservation / raising issues for the first time on appeal

Appellate courts typically do not consider arguments not properly presented to the district court. Recusal arguments, in particular, are ordinarily raised by motion when the issue arises.

Conclusion

Davison v. Bisignano reinforces two procedural pillars in Social Security litigation and appellate practice: (1) benefits-related claims must proceed through § 405(g) and require well-pleaded allegations showing administrative exhaustion, and (2) on appeal, even pro se litigants must develop arguments that directly confront the district court’s dispositive reasoning, or risk waiver and affirmance. The dismissal without prejudice preserves the claimant’s ability to refile, but only if he can properly plead a jurisdictional basis consistent with the Social Security Act’s exclusive review scheme.

text:
The Trump administration began construction on a portion of the U.S.-Mexico border wall cutting through southwest Texas’s Big Bend region despite local leaders’ pushback against the project.

Customs and Border Protection (CBP) told the Associated Press Friday that installation of 30-foot panels was already underway along this portion southern border. The construction started earlier this week, with the agency posted a photo to its website appearing to show a crane lifting one piece of the wall into place.

Big Bend is located on the bend of the Rio Grande and is known for its mountain range, river canyons and desert landscape; it is also home to an eponymous national park. There are five total projects in the region, with the Hudspeth County project being called “Big Bend 1″ on CBP’s website.

CBP added that it is not planning to construct a wall in “Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.”

A federal judge paused Big Bend projects 2 and 4 until the end of September to “allow for additional public engagement.”

Local leaders and residents of Big Bend have expressed concern that the border wall projects will infringe on landowners’ rights. They also fear its presence will diminish its national park, in turn, impacting the economy.

Clara Benson, the founder of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition, told the AP she had received reports of construction supplies moving into the regions, adding her group would “continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is.”

“We will continue fighting to the end,” Benson said, per the AP. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

Yolanda Alvarado, a local cattle rancher and regional director for advocacy group No Big Bend Wall, said, “Our livelihoods are threatened at this point. Not just landowners, but business owners, and not just Big Bend National Park …. it’s everyone in this region.”

In March, bipartisan sheriffs from five counties wrote a letter to federal and state officials opposing the wall in the region. More recently, outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) urged federal officials to meet with stakeholders about the issue.

CBP did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

text:
By Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump has extended an executive order that would impose a fee of $100,000 for H-1B non-immigrant visas by another year, the White ​House said on Friday.

US employers seeking to hire skilled ‌foreign workers can use the federal government’s H-1B visa program for a fee, allowing tech and other professionals from abroad to work in the United States for a few years.

Trump, who has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown, ‌has ​criticized the program and wants to permanently ⁠raise the fee from between $2,000 ⁠and $5,000 to at least $100,000, though the attempt has faced legal challenges.

A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing a June decision by a federal judge who deemed the higher fee imposed by ​the Trump administration illegal and blocked the government from collecting it. Another court is considering whether a judge properly rejected ⁠a challenge to the fee by ⁠the US Chamber of Commerce, the largest US business ​lobbying group.

Trump’s initial order for a fee hike, first released in September 2025, was ​set to expire this month. It did not apply ‌to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, or to renewals of current visas.

Despite criticism that ⁠some companies use the visas to hire lower-paid foreign workers instead of Americans, business groups and companies say they help recruit highly skilled professionals ⁠and address a ‌lack of qualified US workers in some industries.

The ⁠visas, established by Congress in 1990, are ​especially critical ‌for tech companies seeking to recruit from India ​and China.

Changes ⁠to how potential visa holders are scrutinized and processed have impacted companies’ hiring and expansion plans, with some top H-1B users, such as Google parent company Alphabet, moving to increase operations in India.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Daphne Psaledakis, Will Dunham ​and Sergio Non)

text:
A US Federal Appeals Court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by the Trump administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.

Ruling in a case that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful.

The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due-process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

“This decision confirms that due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings,” Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said.

Under President Donald Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a

project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The government is expected to appeal. Earlier in the case, the administration twice convinced the Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants’ due-process rights, clearing the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

The administration has also carried out third-country deportations of people to nations including Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia and the Central African Republic.

DHS General Counsel James Percival posted on X that the policy remains in force because the 1st Circuit’s decision is not yet in effect.

“If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere,” he said.
