text:
The NAACP filed a lawsuit on Sept. 18 asking a judge to prevent the Trump administration from deploying federal agents to polling places in November.

The plaintiffs suing a group of agencies and officials – including the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of Justice and the FBI – allege that sending federal agents to the polls violates the Voting Rights Act because it is an intimidation tactic. The groups say it will result in "voters across the country–particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, naturalized citizens, and members of mixed-status families–are afraid to vote, help others vote, and participate in civic life."

The filing comes after months of federal agents being deployed during primary elections to monitor polls, as recent as earlier in September during the New Hampshire primaries. President Donald Trump has defended his administration's efforts to ensure fair elections and security, and as recent as Sept. 18, Trump continued to claim that he won the 2020 election, in a Truth Social post saying this is third term. In February, USA TODAY reported that the White House said it did not plan to send ICE to polling sites during the midterms.

"Defendants’ past and present actions indicate that they plan to engage in such conduct to attempt to intimidate, or that results in intimidation of, voters in connection with upcoming 2026 elections if they are not enjoined from doing so," the NAACP wrote in the filing.

Trump told reporters in May that he "would do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections" when asked if he would consider sending ICE and the National Guard to polls in November. In July, a group of Democratic senators sent a letter to Trump administration officials to ask if they planned to send federal agents or National Guard to monitor midterm polls.

The National Urban League and American Federation of Teachers are among the plaintiffs in the suit that additionally names DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella, Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and Trump's border czar Tom Homan as defendants. The government did not submit their response to the court before this article was published.

"Congress did not create DHS to oversee elections or determine who is eligible to vote," the NAACP and group of plaintiffs wrote.

Patel testified before Congress' Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 15, and election monitoring was among the various issues he was pressed about by lawmakers. The FBI director would not rule out agents being deployed to polling sites in November.

"If there's a reason to go there because there's been a violation of law, we will, otherwise, we won't," Patel told Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal after explaining that the agency has election-specific crisis coordinators at all of its field offices. He later defended that statement to Democratic Sen. Peter Welch, saying "election integrity is of paramount importance. This FBI is not going to not shy away."

In his confirmation hearing on July 15 before the same committee, Blanche, who leads the Department of Justice, was also pressed on if he would commit to not sending federal agents to polling locations. He said he would "absolutely follow the law no matter what it includes" but did not agree to Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar's characterization of deployments as illegal. Blanche added that he was "not aware of armed agents being at polling places."

"The tap water, it’s not very clean," she said. She added the water smells and leaves stains, and the water has "worms."

The Eloy facility is operated by private prison company CoreCivic, under contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva said Friday that the treatment of ICE detainees is a "moral failure."

A cosmetic surgeon based in Atlanta, Ghasemi found herself being detained in Arizona after she allegedly crossed illegally into the U.S. from Canada. Ghasemi, from Iran and a U.S. resident for years, was denied re-entry by American officials at an airport in Toronto over the summer.

Ghasemi added that facility about 53 miles northwest of Tucson is "super hot." She said the ice machine in her areas has been broken for the last three weeks, and instead, officials with the detention center bring in small cups of ice around 8 p.m.— though they often run out of ice before all the woman can get some.

She added that the women can buy water bottles from the commissary, but the small 6oz bottles—the size of a baseball, she said—each cost $2.

"Water is a mandate at any detention center," she said, adding it takes several days for someone to bring the bottles. "Some of the people don’t have financial support to buy these, much less 7 to 8 bottles per day."

"Unfortunately, no one cares," Ghasemi said.

Dr. Jeffrey Rosenthal, a plastic surgeon based in Connecticut, who advocated for Ghasemi's release while she was in Vermont, said Ghasmi told him when the women in Ghasemi's pod are forced to drink the tap water, they make sure to microwave it, because otherwise "it makes them sick."

A spokesman for CoreCivic said the claims are "inaccurate and do not reflect current facility conditions."

"Individuals in our care always have access to drinking water," he told the Sentinel by email on Friday.

ICE officials did not respond to request for comment from the Sentinel.

'This is a moral failure'

Ghasemi's complaints were echoed by Grijalva, who said ICE detainees at Eloy are facing "deteriorating conditions" including a lack of proper drinking water and broken air conditioning. In a speech on the House floor,, she said her office has "received multiple reports" from family members and attorneys that detainees are "being denied access to proper drinking water. Instead, they are being given one cup of 'ice chips' per day."

This includes a woman diagnosed with leukemia, she said, who told her wife detainees are "only being given ice chips for water, which they have to wait until they melt."

She added two housing blocks are "also without air conditioning."

"This is an outrage," she said.

Grijalva has been stridently critical of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement manages its detention facilities, and has repeatedly used her office to inspect facilities in Arizona—as well as facility in Texas where families with children are held.

In February, she visited the Eloy facility and had what she called a heartbreaking" visit with a 79-year-old grandmother who remained in detention for nine months despite increasing concerns from family members that she suffers from dementia. That woman was later released after Grijalva's urging.

"At least 57 people have already died in ICE custody this year – 4 of them in Arizona. This number is likely higher. How many more human beings need to die before we do something?" Grijalva said.

Advocates warned that should this pace continue, 2026 will be the deadliest year for immigration detainees on record.

"This is a moral failure," Grijalva said. "I’m calling on DHS to immediately address these conditions and ensure that all detainees have access to safe drinking water, edible food, and humane living conditions.”

The Eloy facility was built in 1994 and can hold more than 1,550 people. While it was built to hold people in criminal custody, it has evolved what the Detention Watch Network called the "deadliest immigration detention center in the U.S."

In July, a group of 120 detainees at the facility in Eloy wrote an open letter criticizing the facility, including a range of "human rights abuses," the Arizona Republic reported. The detainees said they experienced verbal and physical abuse by guards, and when they complained about poor conditions they were sent to solitary confinement, or "The Hole."

"The human rights situation at the Eloy Detention Center is appalling and utterly deplorable, with high levels of discrimination by the CoreCivic employees responsible for custody at the center," the detainees wrote, adding "many of the CoreCivic employees are unfit for their jobs because, having a degree of authority over us, they abuse the power through malpractice and policies that harm the detainees."

Threatened with execution by Iranian police for supporting protesters

The Iranian-born Ghasemi landed in the U.S. immigration detention system after she flew from her home in Atlanta, where she has lived since 2019, to speak at the launch of a biotech company in Toronto.

While Ghasemi was granted to ability to travel, including to Iran, by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in 2023, in February 2025, officials rejected her work visa, claiming she had used a false birthdate.

She challenged this finding and stayed in the U.S. for the next year, but on May 27, U.S. immigration officials at the Toronto airport did not allow her through security.

Ghasemi later tried to cross into the U.S. twice more, first at the border crossing at Niagara Falls and again at a border crossing in Michigan. U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers decided she was inadmissible and issued an expedited removal order and banned her from reentering the U.S. for five years.

On June 26, Ghasemi crossed into the U.S. in Vermont and was arrested with an Iranian man. A Border Patrol agent said they were wet and muddy, and were waiting for someone to pick them up after they allegedly crossed into the U.S. on foot, according to court records.

Ghasemi told the Tucson Sentinel she had crossed the border illegally, and she spent nearly 25 days in custody before she agreed to plead guilty to illegal entry.

Ghasemi said she told CBP officials she feared going back to Iran where she was arrested and held in the notorious Evin prison, known for the systematic torture of political prisoners.

Ghasemi told the Sentinel she tried to help during a series of protests in 2022 when Iranian police shot nearly 600 activists with rubber bullets, intentionally blinding them. She said dozens of people lost their eyes, and she later handed then-President Joe Biden a letter.

For this, the Iranian government decided to punish her, kidnapping her when she returned to Tehran after the death of her sister.

She told the Sentinel she was repeatedly blinded and officials threatened to execute her, accusing her of spying for the U.S. She said she tried to kill herself while in solitary there, and she remained anxious and paralyzed.

"Evin is the last point, it’s the last stage for people," she said.

Iranian officials released her on probation.

She said when CBP officials held her Michigan, her post-traumatic stress from this experience returned, and she said she signed the expedited removal document after she spent 10 hours in a holding area, staying in holding from 12:30-10:30 p.m.

She said she told them she had PTSD and was claustrophobic "but, they didn’t care about that."

"They forced me," she said, adding agents told her "'if you don’t sign this, you will stay in this room.'"

"I was paralyzed, and they didn’t care about what I was talking about. I was terrified," Ghasemi said.

While she was in Vermont, an attorney filed a habeas corpus petition, asking a federal judge to order ICE to release her while her immigration case continued.

However, on August 6, that request was rejected and she was later transferred to an ICE detention facility in Louisiana, and then the Florence Service Processing Center in Arizona where she slept on the floor along with dozens of other women.

Food is 'awful'

Ghasemi also criticized the food and what she called "prolonged lockdowns" at the facility.

"The food is awful," she said, adding that one woman from India is on a vegetarian diet, and she was serve moldy bread. She said officials told the woman to "remove the mold and you can eat the rest of the bread."

"We don’t even have vegetables," Ghasemi said, adding that milk for coffee is powdered milk.

She compared the Eloy Detention Center to a facility when she was held in Vermont where the food was cooked by chefs and those held there received milk.

"The food really tasted of food there," she said. "The food here does not taste like food at all."

Ghasemi said there was about 49 women in her part of the facility, or pod, including other women from Iran, four people from Indian and six people from China—including a women who worked as assistant professor at an Arizona university. There are also three Russians held at the facility.

She said the Iranian women have been at the facility for 18 months, or more, a consequence of the Trump administration's drive to make detention mandatory for nearly everyone. Further, the Laken Riley Act increased mandatory detention by allowing the administration to hold people "not only convicted of but charged with or arrested for crimes such as shoplifting to detention without a bond hearing."

"This latest statutory expansion is the culmination of decades of expanding immigrant detention," according to the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

Ghasemi said the food was making some people diabetic, while others faced higher blood pressure, hair loss, and problems with their gums and teeth. She said one woman had been in the facility for nearly 19 months along with her husband and lost 30 pounds because of a lack of good food and stress.

Ghasemi also criticized medical care at the facility, telling the Sentinel she helped treat a woman who had a tooth extracted. The woman was left with an abscess, which Ghasemi helped treat by draining it. She said the wound "smelled," but officials at the detention center did not give her antibiotics, but instead just mouthwash.

In March, Emmanuel Cleeford Damas, 56, died at a Scottsdale hospital weeks after he complained of a toothache while in custody at the nearby Florence Correctional Center. A preliminary report from the Maricopa County Medical Examiner said Damas died from "complications of necrotizing mediastinitis with neck and retropharyngeal abscess in the setting of severe dental caries and periodontal disease."

Necrotizing mediastinitis is a rare, life-threatening complication caused by an abscess in the deep issues behind the back of the throat.

In June, ICE decided to stop reporting deaths of people who die within 30 days of their release, a move immigration advocates and health professionals warned will make it harder to understand rising problems with health care inside the immigration detention system and it comes after federal watchdogs were effectively dismantled. Authorities could release someone about to die from a critical illness or injury, and that would not be counted as a detention-related death in the agency's statistics.

Ghasemi said another woman suffered seizures, and officers refused to help and instead tried to lockdown their area. She said she, and a woman from China, treated her for low blood pressure.

The complaints about the facility come as detainees are spending more time there—some over a year—because the Trump administration has sought to deport them to countries they had never lived. More than half were detained more than six months, passing a measure the Supreme Court said could violate the constitution, according to an analysis by the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting.

Earlier this year, the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project said they are seeing an "alarming increase" in the number of people in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody facing "potentially life-threatening medical neglect."

The nonprofit group offers legal and social services, and advocates for the civil rights of immigrants being held in Arizona, including those at the Central Arizona Florence Correctional Center, the Florence Service Processing Center, and the Eloy Detention Center.

This includes people who have "severe medical issues or chronic illnesses," and they group attributed this to ICE's move to "detain everyone, regardless of their medical history, regardless of whether they can obtain the medical care they need in ICE custody, and regardless of how unsafe detention conditions would be for them."

Ryan Gustin, a spokesman for CoreCivic, said the allegations regarding drinking water and air conditioning are "inaccurate and do not reflect current facility conditions."

"Individuals in our care always have access to drinking water," he said.

He said the "safety, health and well-being of the individuals entrusted to our care, and our nearly 350 staff members, is our top priority."

"We take seriously our obligation to comply with all applicable federal detention standards and to maintain a safe, secure and humane environment for those in our care at the Eloy Detention Center," Gustin said. "Facility operations are subject to significant oversight and accountability, including regular audits, inspections and monitoring by our government partners."

"We are not aware of any ongoing air-conditioning outage affecting housing units, and facility leadership has confirmed that the HVAC system is operating properly," Gustin said. "We have no recent record of maintenance issues affecting housing unit temperatures."

He said the facility has "established maintenance protocols and contingency measures in place" in case a system fails.

Gustin said the company provides "three nutritious meals daily, with menus reviewed and approved by a registered dietitian. Accommodations are made for religious, therapeutic and cultural dietary needs."

"We have a robust grievance process that provides multiple avenues for individuals in our care to raise concerns, and we investigate issues brought to our attention," Gustin said. "At this time, we are not aware of grievances substantiating the allegations outlined in your inquiry."

text:
“Operation Metro Surge” — the Trump administration’s deployment of thousands of immigration agents to Minnesota last winter — left two citizens dead, more than 4,000 people arrested and communities roiled with protests. The city’s education system, one teacher said, became “hunting grounds” which saw agents “follow brown children home.”

The resulting climate of fear from the three-month operation disrupted the critical window when students prepare for state standardized tests, educators said. The Minnesota Comprehensive Assessments measure academic proficiency across grades 3 through 8 and high school.

The test results will come out later this month and school communities are bracing for a significant decline in student performance. Meanwhile, educators are still navigating the fallout from Metro Surge, and what Mandi Jung, a St. Paul middle school science teacher, described in a video clip circulated widely online as a “mass psychosis” among students.

“We started this school year with thousands of students that we had in our schools last year just gone,” Jung said in the video, addressing Minnesota teachers. “There was no ‘how to heal from an occupation by the federal government’ where schools were directly targeted.”

She added: “Legislators couldn’t even get an ICE ban in schools passed last year when we knew that the feds were using schools as stakeouts, as hunting grounds, as places to follow brown children home.”

For many families, that fear became an immediate reality. Children looked on as parents were dragged from homes, workplaces and vehicles, while federal enforcement routinely used school perimeters and neighborhood drop-off zones as surveillance stakeouts.

The crisis drew national attention on January 20, 2026, when masked ICE agents in Columbia Heights detained five-year-old Valley View Elementary pre-kindergarten student Liam Conejo Ramos and his father in their driveway as they arrived home from school. A widely-circulated photo of Liam in his rabbit beanie and Spiderman backpack became the heartbreaking symbol of a campaign that swept up young children and families.

Last December, thousands of Department of Homeland Security agents, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection officers, were deployed to the Twin Cities area and surrounding communities.

According to a June report by Human Rights Watch, the operation was marked by “racial profiling, harassment, and surveillance” that left communities deeply fractured. During the operation, two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by agents.

Despite official claims to be targeting violent offenders, Human Rights Watch found that nearly two out of three immigrants arrested by ICE during the operation had no prior U.S. criminal history.

The report also noted that federal agents “spread terror and fear” and “terrorized” Minnesotans, “chilling their rights to freedom of expression and assembly, and impacting their rights to education and health.”

Despite intense pushback from local school boards, superintendents and public protests demanding no enforcement near schools, the Department of Homeland Security defended the tactics.

“Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear,” a DHS spokesperson told The Independent. “ICE does not target schools. This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement who are facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them and an 8,000% increase in death threats.

“ICE is not going to schools to arrest children — we are protecting children. Criminals are no longer able to hide in America’s schools to avoid arrest. The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement and instead trusts them to use common sense. If a dangerous illegal alien felon were to flee into a school, or a child sex offender is working as an employee, there may be a situation where an arrest is made to protect public safety.”

Months later, educators expect to see further impacts from Operation Metro Surge on their students. Union leaders shared Jung’s concerns, warning that standard testing measures would inevitably reflect the collective trauma of the federal raids.

“We don’t expect the state government to pause in the accountability system as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic,” Education Minnesota President Monica Byron told The Independent.

“But we hope state officials and journalists will present education data from the 2025-26 school year into the proper context after the massive disruption to learning caused by the federal government’s actions.”

Anticipating pushback that attributes lower scores strictly to school quality, Byron also cautioned against oversimplified metrics.

“It’s normal for parents to want honest feedback, but political actors with little understanding of standardized tests make all sorts of wild claims about what the scores mean,” Byron said. “Our message to parents is what it has always been: Talk to your child’s educators, who always know more about the student's strengths and challenges than any bubble test.”

Other local teachers also shared the psychological toll and widespread disruption caused by federal immigration enforcement on the children in their care.

“I had students that would say, ‘I just need to go in your back room and cry,’ and they did during class,” Stacy Bartlett, a veteran biology teacher from Stillwater, told KSTP-TV.

Bartlett, who helps write the MCA biology exam, said she noticed a clear shift in classroom dynamics during Operation Metro Surge, with diminished student focus and falling attendance.

“In January, there was a quiet. It’s hard to describe, but they were quiet, and I knew that it was bothering them, and I knew they didn’t have the words to talk about it, and so I would say every single student was affected in one way or another,” she said.

Across 29 Minnesota school districts and charter schools with high populations of English language learners, midyear enrollment fell by approximately 1,700 students between October 2025 and March 2026.

That compared to a decline of fewer than 80 students during the same period the previous year, according to data from Sahan Journal and MPR News.

Minneapolis and St. Paul public school districts each lost nearly 500 students midyear. In suburban districts like Fridley, which serves a significant immigrant and refugee population, the number of students dropped from rosters due to 15 consecutive unexcused absences tripled compared to the previous year.

“Kids literally disappeared,” Fridley Public Schools Superintendent Brenda Lewis told Sahan Journal and MPR News. “Literally in an unprecedented manner. Overnight.”

Bartlett recounted that the immense distress led some students to give up during tests, either shutting down their digital exam software mid-test or rapidly clicking through questions without reading them.

A survey of 4,460 educators conducted online this spring on behalf of Education Minnesota, the state teachers’ union, revealed the extent of the upheaval.

Some 72 percent of polled members reported being directly or indirectly impacted by Operation Metro Surge — a figure that rose to 93 percent among Twin Cities educators, where enforcement was most heavily concentrated.

According to the survey, roughly two-thirds of teachers observed increased absenteeism along with heightened student fear and anxiety, while nearly half reported students becoming noticeably withdrawn. In the Twin Cities metro area, nearly 90 percent of educators reported elevated fear and attendance drops.

The long-term toll on those displaced students remains a critical concern for teachers.

“It’s hard to quantify the lasting damage to students so early in the school year, but we know there was a mental health crisis among young people before Operation Metro Surge,” Byron said. “We assume the violent tactics used by ICE agents in January and February worsened it. There are simply not enough mental health resources for children in Minnesota during normal times, much less now.

“Of course, there’s another question about whether the 1,700 students who left Minnesota public schools and didn’t return are receiving any care at all. I hope they are.”

At St. Paul’s Battle Creek Middle School, social studies teacher Alli Kildahl recalled the moment students returned to in-person classes following a temporary shift to remote learning during the peak of Operation Metro Surge.

“When that initial burst of joy faded, we looked around and realized we’re still missing a lot of kids,” Kildahl told Sahan Journal and MPR News. “A lot of them slowly trickled back over the next month or two. And some of them are still not anywhere to be found.”

To address the secondary trauma that educators faced, Education Minnesota partnered with the National Education Association and the American Federation of Teachers to provide counseling and mental health training.

“We’re rarely asked about the mental health of educators even though workplaces that are burning out good people are among the very top challenges facing public education in Minnesota,” Byron told The Independent. “Is all of that enough? I worry that it is not.”

As the Minnesota Department of Education prepares to publish the 2025-2026 assessment data, Byron confirmed Education Minnesota will issue an official response.

text:
The advertising blitzkrieg of L.A.’s mayoral campaign is here.

Mayor Karen Bass and her opponent, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, dropped new campaign commercials over the last week, buying time on television, streaming channels and other platforms. Supporters of both candidates released ads as well.

The two candidates relied heavily on free media for most of the summer, putting videos on Instagram and inviting the news media to cover their appearances.

The dam effectively burst on Monday, with Raman touting her new Hollywood-themed ad “For Your Consideration,” timed to coincide with the Emmy Awards.

The 30-second spot starts with Raman stepping out on the town, then shifts to some standard L.A. imagery: freeways, palm trees, Echo Park Lake and, of course, the Hollywood sign.

“L.A. shows the world what it means to be a star,” declares the ad’s narrator, actor and screenwriter Bob Odenkirk. “And every Angeleno deserves the chance to reach for their own.”

After Raman has stopped off at a taco stand and hugged a dog, Odenkirk delivers the ad’s final message: “Change. Affordability. An L.A. that loves you back.”

That ad ran on television a few times before being cycled onto social media, per the Raman campaign.

Three days later, Bass went up with a 30-second spot — on digital platforms for now — centered on President Trump’s immigration raids.

The ad offers footage from the day in July 2025 when Bass confronted federal immigration agents in MacArthur Park. The video features images of gun-toting federal agents in military uniforms and Bass hopping out of a car in an aquamarine pant suit to face them.

“When someone comes after your family, you don’t hesitate,” Bass says. “You stand up. You fight.”

One of Bass’ most formidable allies — the Los Angeles Police Protective League — went hard negative with its first ad of the runoff campaign, offering the message that Raman “Doesn’t Get It.”

The commercial, released Friday, follows a young girl as she walks past a homeless encampment, juxtaposed against video of Raman talking about her opposition to a law that prohibits encampments near schools.

“I don’t think a kid’s gonna be safer because a tent is 500 feet away from a school,” Raman said in the clip, which was taken from a 2024 candidate forum in Sherman Oaks.

The backpack-wearing child speaks to the camera and says: “Walking to school shouldn’t be scary.”

“I’m just a kid,” she says. “But even I know I’d be safer if this was 500 feet away.”

The police union says the ad will start running on television this weekend and already is on social media platforms.

Meanwhile, Raman’s backers have an assortment of attack ads running on Facebook and Instagram.

Streets For All, a group that wants to expand the city’s bus and bike lane network, pulled video footage from a different Sherman Oaks candidate forum — this one featuring Bass and Raman last month.

At that event, Bass told the audience that Raman is unresponsive to her constituents, forcing many in Sherman Oaks to contact the mayor’s office directly.

“Many of you have my cellphone, you have called me,” Bass says in the ad. “You called on me specifically for help.”

Streets For All contends those remarks show that Bass gives wealthy homeowners her number while “regular Angelenos get ignored.”

“L.A. deserves a mayor who doesn’t just listen to the rich and powerful,” the ad says.

By Friday, Streets For All had nearly two dozen different video spots opposing Bass over such issues as homelessness, transparency and the Palisades fire, according to Ethics Commission filings.

The biggest backer of the group’s political action committee is hedge fund manager Aaron Sosnick. Of the $1.2 million that the group plans to spend in the mayor’s race, Sosnick has provided $1 million, said Michael Schneider, who heads the group.

Schneider said the committee also has financial support from retired real estate developer Yuval Bar-Zemer — known for his work in the Arts District — and Todd Wexman, chief principal of 4SITE Real Estate, a real estate development company.

Raman pollster says she’s in the lead

The Raman campaign shared the results of a new internal poll that showed their candidate with a five-point lead over Bass.

Of the 600 likely voters who were surveyed, 44% supported Raman and 39% backed Bass, with 17% undecided, according to a memo provided to the campaign and viewed by The Times. The survey, conducted by Hart Research Associates in early September, had a margin of error of 4 percentage points.

“In the initial trial heat for Los Angeles mayor, Councilmember Nithya Raman is in the rare position for a challenger of already LEADING the incumbent,” the polling firm wrote.

Another poll, commissioned by an independent expenditure group supporting Raman, portrayed the race as a statistical tie, at least initially. Estamos con Nithya for Mayor of LA 2026, sponsored by the Western States Regional Council of Carpenters, said its poll showed Bass with 38% and Raman at 37%.

However, when voters received more information on the candidates, Raman took a 7-percentage-point lead, with 41% supporting her and 34% supporting Bass, according to a memo prepared by the group’s pollster.

The margin of error was 3.7 percentage points.

The Bass campaign declined to share its internal polling when contacted by The Times.

However, Neighborhoods for a Better L.A., an independent expenditure group supporting the mayor, said a survey it commissioned in early August showed the mayor with an edge over Raman of 41% to 35%, with 24% of the electorate undecided.

That poll, conducted by Tulchin Research, surveyed 1,200 likely Los Angeles voters and has a 2.8-percentage-point margin of error, the group said.

The poll also found that when given “balanced biographies” about both candidates, Bass’ support grew to 45% while Raman went down to 33%.

“Communications focused on Raman’s record can both reduce her support and consolidate voters behind Bass,” the pollsters wrote.

Giving back El Grito cash

Los Angeles City Councilmember Imelda Padilla locked down sponsorships for the city’s celebration of El Grito, which marks Mexico’s independence.

Tuesday’s event, which featured an evening of musical performances, was sponsored by an assortment of city contractors and government agencies, including waste hauler Athens Services and the Department of Water and Power.

Still, Padilla decided she didn’t want to partner with one particular business, announcing at the last minute that organizers no longer would accept a $5,000 sponsorship from Home Depot.

On the day of the celebration, Padilla issued an apology on Instagram, saying she had heard from community members upset over the event’s affiliation with Home Depot, whose parking lots have been the site of many federal immigration raids.

“We have rescinded their partnership for this event,” Padilla said in her post. “The spirit of El Grito is rooted in celebrating our Latino heritage and creating a space where our families feel welcomed, safe, and celebrated.”

In an email, a Home Depot spokesperson said the company is not involved in immigration enforcement activities and doesn’t coordinate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement or U.S. Border Patrol. The company also doesn’t receive advance warning about enforcement actions, the representative said.

“We cannot legally interfere with federal enforcement agencies, including preventing them from coming into our stores and parking lots,” Home Depot spokesperson Evelyn Fornes said.

State of play

— COZY WITH CARUSO: Billionaire developer Rick Caruso, who was defeated by Bass in 2022, appeared alongside the mayor at a groundbreaking for the Palisades Recreation Center. Caruso praised her for her work on the project but stopped short of endorsing, saying he intends to meet with Raman in the coming weeks.

— LIFE AFTER PRATT: The voters who picked reality TV personality Spencer Pratt in the June 2 primary election are now up for grabs. But will they stay home instead of picking a mayoral candidate?

— BASS BAILS: The mayor skipped a congressional hearing on waste and fraud in homeless spending this week, calling the session politically motivated. Rep. Tim Burchett, the Republican who chaired the subcommittee meeting, accused her of dodging accountability.

— FINDING FRAUD: Federal authorities arrested three people who were working in Los Angeles-area homeless nonprofits this week, accusing one of them of misappropriating more than $7.5 million in taxpayer funds. Scott Turner, secretary of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, said the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority, which provided the funding, had allowed fraud to “run rampant.”

— WE’RE IN THE MONEY: The 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles will generate up to $40.6 billion in increased economic output and add as many as 224,000 jobs, according to an upbeat economic forecast released this week. Another, more tempered estimate put the increase at $20.5 billion to $25.4 billion.

— SEETHING OVER SKID ROW: Some activists want dogs taken away from homeless residents living in Skid Row, saying those animals are living in an unsafe environment. A Bass aide responded by cautioning that it is “neither humane nor legal to remove animals from their human companions without appropriate cause.”

QUICK HITS

Where is Inside Safe? The mayor’s signature program to combat homelessness went to Avalon Boulevard and 64th Street in South L.A., an area represented by Councilmember Curren Price.

On the docket next week: The council’s Public Works Committee meets Tuesday to discuss ways of cleaning, safeguarding or demolishing nuisance properties.

title: Trump Blasts Supreme Court Over Tariff and Birthright Citizenship Rulings - Newsweek
description:
President Donald Trump criticized the U.S. Supreme Court on Saturday, accusing the justices of issuing "faulty, political, and ridiculous decisions" on tariffs and birthright citizenship that he claimed have cost the United States "trillions of dollars."
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote the court had "lacked the Courage to MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN" and argued that its rulings on tariffs and birthright citizenship had damaged the country economically and altered how citizenship is granted in the country.

text:
President Donald Trump criticized the U.S. Supreme Court on Saturday, accusing the justices of issuing "faulty, political, and ridiculous decisions" on tariffs and birthright citizenship that he claimed have cost the United States "trillions of dollars." The president's comments mark his latest public attack on the high court following major defeats on two signature policies of his second term.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote the court had "lacked the Courage to MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN" and argued that its rulings on tariffs and birthright citizenship had damaged the country economically and altered how citizenship is granted in the country.

"Over the last 6 months, with their faulty, political, and ridiculous decisions on TARIFFS and Birthright Citizenship, they have cost the United States of America Trillions of Dollars, and forever damaged the way people become Citizens of our great Country," Trump wrote.

Read More on News

Newsweek reached out to the White House for comment on Saturday.

Why It Matters

The post targets two of the most consequential legal setbacks of Trump's presidency. In February, the court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give Trump authority to impose sweeping global tariffs, forcing the administration to unwind the policy and issue refunds to importers. The administration later pursued alternative tariff authorities, like Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose 10 to 12.5 percent tariffs on imports from 60 U.S. trading partners, after the court struck down the original duties. The Section 301 tariffs are currently facing legal challenges.

According to documents filed by customs officials with the U.S. Court of International Trade and cited by the Financial Times, the Trump administration, as of August, has paid around $100 billion in tariff refunds to importers. That represents roughly 60 percent of the $166 billion that businesses are estimated to have paid in tariffs.

The court also dealt Trump a major setback in June when it upheld a broad interpretation of birthright citizenship and rejected his effort to limit automatic citizenship for many children born in the U.S. to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the country. The justices relied on longstanding interpretations of the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause.

Conservative Justice Clarence Thomas dissented, writing that he was not convinced the court's interpretation of the Citizenship Clause would "stand the test of time."

The decisions nevertheless came from a court with a conservative majority that includes three Trump appointees: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

Trump argued that the rulings had harmed the economy and immigration policy.

"It has been a sad chapter in the life and times of America, but we will prevail!" the president wrote Saturday.

The Birthright Citizenship Fight Continues

The administration continues to pursue other avenues aimed at restricting birthright citizenship and combating what it describes as birth tourism.

Earlier this month, a federal judge blocked enforcement of a new Trump administration order seeking to restrict birthright citizenship, ruling that the government could not deny citizenship to a class of children whom the Supreme Court had already determined are citizens at birth. According to the ruling, the Supreme Court's decision established that children born in the U.S. to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the country are protected by the Fourteenth Amendment.

In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote: "The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are 'citizens at birth.' ... The President must follow it."

The court's June ruling was authored by Chief Justice John Roberts, who wrote that birthright citizenship extends to "every free-born person in this land" and concluded: "We keep that promise today."

The administration has also issued separate directives aimed at preventing foreign nationals from traveling to the U.S. primarily to give birth and secure citizenship for their children, a strategy that officials have emphasized after the Supreme Court defeat.

Trump and his allies have shown little sign of abandoning the issue since the court's June decision. In recent weeks, the administration unveiled new executive orders targeting birth tourism and other categories it argues fall outside traditional birthright citizenship protections, while conservative activists have discussed ways to keep the debate alive through future litigation, legislation and judicial nominations, including efforts to shape future judicial candidates.

What Happens Next

Trump's comments do not announce any new legal action or policy initiative, but they show his continued frustration with rulings that curtailed two of his highest-profile initiatives. While the administration has sought alternative legal pathways on both tariffs and immigration, the court's decisions remain major constraints on the president's agenda.

The White House has not immediately indicated whether Trump is seeking additional legislative or legal remedies in response to either ruling.

title: Trump starts building wall in Big Bend, Texas, despite landowner, business and rancher opposition
description:
Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1.
There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.
Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.
In Texas, much of the opposition has centered on the agency’s plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state’s southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world.
Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.
text:
The start of construction marks an important milestone in the administration’s $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology as it seeks to make good on a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump to finish the wall. And it comes as Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace at which it is building the wall across the U.S.-Mexico border.

Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.

CBP said the first panels were erected on September 15. On a map on the agency’s website where the agency posts updates of wall construction across the entire southern border, a photo showed a crane lifting one of the 30-foot-tall steel wall panels into place while construction workers looked on.

The new activity was separate from a border infrastructure project in the nearby Big Bend National Park, where the administration has temporarily suspended construction in an attempt to reach out to opponents.

Activist plan to keep up their fight

In the broader Big Bend region of Texas, CBP has run up against concerted opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote region isn’t a high-traffic area for illegal immigration.

Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.

Clara Benson, one of the founders of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition which has been fighting against CBP’s plans, said in an interview Friday that the organization had been receiving reports of trucks moving supplies into the remote area along the Rio Grande and that contractors had been clearing yards to stage supplies.

But speaking from Washington, D.C. where she and others in the coalition were meeting with lawmakers, she said that the organization and others would continue to fight the wall-building plans across the region.

“We will continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is. We will continue fighting to the end,” said Benson. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

Trump has vowed to complete the border wall

The news comes as the administration is speeding forward with a plan to line the entire border with a combination of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, barriers designed to stop vehicles from crossing the border, new patrol roads, and various technologies to deter and detect migrants or smugglers from crossing the border.

Customs and Border Protection said it is building an average of 12 miles of barriers per week along the 2,000-mile border with Mexico and recently reached a milestone of 200 miles of new barriers built since the second Trump administration took office.

The 12-miles-a-week average is double the pace that the agency’s head, Rodney Scott, cited earlier this year.

The agency has faced opposition from environmental groups, a small town that worries the wall will cause flooding in its area, Native Americans who say the construction is disturbing sacred sites and landowners who say the construction will infringe on their land.

In Texas, much of the opposition has centered on the agency’s plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state’s southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world. But up and downriver outside the park, much of the land is owned by private landowners, many of whom have pushed back against the government’s efforts.

Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.

Activists and landowners have also shown up at county meetings to push their elected officials not to cooperate with contractors hired by CBP to build the wall, and many landowners have refused to allow government officials or contractors onto their land to survey it.

title: Exiled Nicaraguan journalist detained by ICE in Florida. He could be deported
description:

His wife, Deykel Santamaría, told El Nuevo Herald, that her husband applied for political asylum in 2019 and that the case remains pending.

text:
Press-freedom groups and South Florida members of Congress are calling on federal immigration authorities to release exiled Nicaraguan journalist Luis Manuel Chavarría-Galeano after he was detained Monday by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Florida.

His detention is sparking fears that his life would be put in danger if he is deported to Nicaragua under the authoritarian regime of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega and his wife and co-President Rosario Murillo.

Chavarría-Galeano, 48, was arrested on the morning of Sept. 14 while working as an Uber/Lyft driver in Orlando. He was then transferred to the Baker Correctional Facility in north Florida and later sent to the Krome North Service Processing Center in west Miami-Dade County.

He remains in custody at Krome pending an Oct. 2 immigration hearing, WLRN confirmed late Friday.

His wife, Deykel Santamaría, told El Nuevo Herald, that her husband applied for political asylum in 2019 and that the case remains pending.

“My husband has a very substantial asylum application file and a book of testimonies from a journalist who has been very outspoken against all the policies of the Ortega-Murillo regime,” Santamaría told the Spanish-language newspaper in Miami.

In a statement to El Pais newspaper in Spain, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said ICE agents arrested Chavarría-Galeano “during routine immigration enforcement operations” because he was “unlawfully present in the United States.”

The DHS spokesperson said Chavarría-Galeano entered the U.S. legally on December 21, 2018, and overstayed his visa, which ended on June 20, 2019.

“In violation of our nation’s laws, he remained in the country beyond the authorized period,” the DHS spokesman said. “He will remain in ICE custody while his removal proceedings are processed.”

It’s unclear if Chavarría-Galeano would be deported to Nicaragua or Spain. He also holds Spanish citizenship.

“I am strengthened in faith,” Chavarría-Galeano told Telemundo 31, a Spanish-language station in Orlando late Friday in a brief phone interview.

Speaking in Spanish, he also said he would not wish what he is experiencing at the ICE detention center on anyone.

Press-freedom advocates sound the alarm

Press-freedom organizations have urged federal immigration authorities to immediately release Chavarría-Galeano and review his pending asylum application, saying he would face persecution if returned to Nicaragua.

“This detention fits into a troubling pattern in which the Trump administration has wielded immigration enforcement against members of the press,” said José Zamora, Américas regional director for the Committee to Protect Journalists.

“It is critical that journalists who have sought asylum in the United States after fleeing persecution for their journalistic work are protected, not treated as targets for immigration enforcement,” Zamora said in a statement.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) raised questions about Chavarría-Galeano’s detention, warning that deporting a targeted journalist back to a hostile regime creates a dangerous precedent for political exiles seeking asylum.

In a statement, Edith Rodríguez Cachera, RSF Spain’s vice president, said Spanish government officials “must use every diplomatic and consular instrument at its disposal to safeguard his security and prevent his return to a country where he will likely be targeted due to his journalistic work.”

She said the Spanish government granted citizenship to Chavarría-Galeano in July 2025.

In a joint statement released Friday, the Miami-based Inter American Press Association, along with 14 other press-freedom organizations, demanded Chavarría-Galeano’s immediate release.. They also pushed for an asylum hearing.

“The U.S. government’s targeting and detention of [Chavarría-Galeano] are a troubling escalation of attacks on journalists and media workers, particularly immigrant journalists, who consistently provide much-needed journalism and civic information for their communities,” the 15 press groups wrote in their statement.

Santamaría, Chavarría-Galeano’s wife, told El Pais: “I fear for his safety, his freedom and his integrity if he were to be sent to Nicaragua. ... He could be sent back into the hands of the same regime he fled to protect his life and his freedom.”

South Florida lawmakers: He is a political exile — not a criminal

U.S. Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Miami, urged the Trump administration to “enforce the [immigration] law and deport dangerous individuals, but do not treat political exiles like criminals.”

“Luis is a respected journalist who paid a price for telling the truth about the Ortega-Murillo dictatorship,” she wrote on X. “The regime persecuted him, forced him into exile, and stripped him of his citizenship.”

“That history matters,” she said. “He cannot be sent back into the hands of the people who targeted him.”

U.S. Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, R-Miami, posted on X that he was “deeply troubled” by the detention of Chavarría-Galeano, saying the U.S. “must never lose sight of the difference between criminals and people fleeing political repression.”

Persecuted in Nicaragua for being a journalist

Chavarría-Galeano began work as a journalist in Nicaragua in the late 1990s. In 2012, he established Café con Voz, a prominent political commentary and news program that aired on the independent TV channel 100% Noticias, according to media reports.

In December 2018, following widespread anti-government protests, the Ortega regime launched a sweeping crackdown on independent media. Police raided the offices of 100% Noticias, arresting channel owner Miguel Mora and press director Lucía Pineda.

Chavarría-Galeano narrowly escaped arrest — he was out of the country on vacation at the time. He sought political asylum upon arriving in the United States on December 21, 2018, filing his formal asylum petition in 2019, according to press-freedom groups and Chavarría-Galeano’s wife.

While living in exile, Galeano continued to produce Café con Voz on YouTube and report on human-rights abuses in Nicaragua.

In 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists, Chavarría-Galeano was among 94 Nicaraguans stripped of their citizenship by the Ortega government, which accused them of being “traitors to the homeland” and ordered the confiscation of their assets.

CPJ staffers said they have documented Nicaragua’s press-freedom crisis, saying 268 Nicaraguan journalists were kicked out of the country into exile, with many living in neighboring Costa Rica.

Under the Ortega-Murillo regime, the government has carried out a sweeping crackdown on dissent following a violent suppression of protests in 2018. Authorities have jailed opposition politicians, religious leaders and others, and also shut down thousands of civil-society organizations.

The congress has repeatedly amended the constitution to concentrate power in Ortega’s hands and eliminate any shred of democratic independence and dissent.

This report was supplemented with information from The Associated Press and produced by Miami Herald news partner WLRN Public Media.

text:
How far will New York Gov. Kathy Hochul go to keep immigrant criminals in this country?

So far, she’ll even pardon a man convicted of an aggravated felony, if that’s what it takes to prevent the United States Supreme Court from setting a restrictionist precedent.

Keisy Guerrero Mariano is a Dominican who spent two years in prison for committing a violent crime: second-degree assault.

Mariano, known as “G.M.” in court documents, is exactly the sort of lawbreaker Americans overwhelmingly want to see deported.

But not Hochul—she granted him clemency on Aug. 28.

His case stood out from those of the other five people she pardoned that day:

The others were nonviolent offenders who’d committed their crimes decades ago: two in the 1980s, two in the ’90s, and just one as recently as 2007.

G.M. was convicted in 2015.

The governor decided he merited special leniency for political reasons.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested G.M. in 2020, intending to deport him based on his criminal record.

ICE had to let him go in 2022, however, because of a nationwide injunction related to COVID-19 that required the agency to review the custody of individuals with certain medical conditions.

While ICE had him, though, G.M.’s lawyers challenged the agency’s right to hold him for a prolonged time without a bond hearing.

That’s what Hochul’s pardon is really about—the Trump administration planned to make the Dominican’s appeals a test case before the Supreme Court, one likely to establish that G.M. and others like him are not entitled to a bond hearing.

Bond hearings are an easily exploited weakness in America’s immigration security, not only protracting the legal process of deporting lawbreakers but also giving them an opportunity to get out of detention temporarily—and then permanently fail to show up when they’re due for their next hearing.

G.M. came to this country legally in 2011, but he forfeited any right to remain here once he committed a felony.

Only now Hochul has nullified his conviction to undercut ICE’s grounds for removing him and collapse the appeals process that was leading to the Supreme Court—and to a probable defeat for those who want to make deportation as difficult as possible.

The governor isn’t looking out for New Yorkers here:

Her maneuver is about liberal politicians’ zeal for maximum immigration, even when it means letting violent criminals remain in our communities.

This is the second lucky break Hochul’s side has had recently.

The other test case the Trump administration had teed up, involving a Jamaican national convicted (also in New York) of sexually abusing a child under the age of 11, has been taken out of the courts as well, after the offender left the country and filed a court declaration saying he would not be coming back to America.

Self-deportation is one way to get immigrants convicted of heinous crimes out of here.

But ICE can’t deport someone who has already deported himself, so his claim of a right to a bond hearing is now completely moot.

The big question still has to be answered, though: Can immigration enforcement detain these violent perps and sex offenders until they can be tossed out?

Or if they’ve been in custody for a while, are they entitled to bond hearings that will further delay their removal—and give them the chance to escape back into Americans’ neighborhoods?

Solicitor General John Sauer says he’s not going to let Hochul’s gambit succeed.

G.M.’s case may have been pulled, but Sauer aims to find another that will bring the fight to the Supreme Court.

“Mandatory deportation” should mean just that—even a legal immigrant who commits a serious offense ought to be expelled promptly, and he shouldn’t get the benefit of a bond hearing just because his case takes longer than it should and he winds up in “prolonged” detention.

He shouldn’t get the benefit of a liberal governor’s partisan machinations, either.

New Yorkers—American citizens—elected Hochul, and she should put them first, not foreigners who commit crimes while they’re here, legally or otherwise.

text:
A coalition of civil rights groups and union organizations Friday sued the Trump administration to prevent the deployment of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling locations during November’s midterm elections.

Earlier this summer, the Trump administration briefly indicated it would not pursue mass ICE enforcement at polling locations before officials reversed course and sparked the wave of lawsuits.

The suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia is the second this month, following comments from top Trump officials citing a federal policy to allow ICE officers to enter polling locations in certain circumstances to conduct immigration enforcement.

The groups argue the policy violates the federal law that prohibits “armed men” at election sites, and also causes voter intimidation, which is barred under the Voting Rights Act.

Under federal law, “troops” or “armed men” are allowed at polling locations only if “such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.” And the section of the Voting Rights Act the groups cite prohibits “intimidation,” “threats,” or “coercion” against a person for voting or attempting to vote.

“The result is predictable: voters across the country—particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, naturalized citizens, and members of mixed-status families—are afraid to vote, help others vote, and participate in civic life,” according to the suit.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin earlier this month noted that agents could conduct immigration enforcement at polling places. And before U.S. senators this week, FBI Director Kash Patel did not rule out sending FBI agents to polling locations, but said officers would “follow the law.”

The Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s requests for comment Friday.

“We reject this administration’s attempt to desecrate our polling sites by converting them into militarized zones through the unlawful deployment of ICE or any other federal agent,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, said in a statement.

NAACP is one of nine groups that filed suit. The rest are Mi Familia en Accion, Asian Pacific American Advocates, the National Urban League, Minnesota 8, the Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of Teachers, the International Union of Painters and the United Food and Commercial Workers International.

“Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period,” Clarke said. “The NAACP calls on the court to reject this blatant attempt by federal officials to obstruct our elections through tactics pulled straight from the Jim Crow playbook.”

ICE said its pursuit of electrified shock gloves is meant to be a less violent option for officers and agents seeking to gain control of unruly individuals, reducing the need to use a Taser, baton or pepper spray.

David Venturella, acting head of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said they have not yet deployed the gloves in the field and are still in the procurement phase.

He said unlike a Taser, which shoots probes at a person, the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, or GLOVE system, would have agents make direct physical contact with a target’s bare skin. It would send “low-level electrical pulses” that would help officers gain compliance.

Mr. Venturella, in a letter to Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, described it as “a lower level of force than other intermediate methods.”

“This technology is intended to provide officers with an additional, controlled option to de-escalate volatile situations,” the ICE chief wrote.

The system made headlines when it was first reported.

ICE critics worried about giving another tool to an agency under fire for its treatment of protesters of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

Mr. Grassley, Iowa Republican, had asked ICE to explain its thinking.

ICE said a pair of gloves would cost $2,495.

When an agent or officer uses the gloves, it would have to be reported as a use-of-force incident. Personnel would get annual training, on top of their quarterly use-of-force training.

The procurement documents for the gloves said they would be available to both Homeland Security Investigations, the agency’s criminal division, and Enforcement and Removal Operations, the deportation force that carries out civil immigration enforcement.

title: Appeals Court Blocks Trump Policy to Rapidly Deport Migrants to Third Countries | Truthout
authors: britney, Ariana Figueroa, Mike Ludwig, Marianne Dhenin, Sharon Zhang, Megan Rose, Andy Mannix, Ibrahim Hirsi, Sonali Kolhatkar, Victoria Valenzuela
description:
Third-country removals, deportations from the United States to a nation other than an immigrant’s home country, occur when the immigrant’s home country does not accept the person’s repatriation.
Once rare, the procedure has spiked under the second Trump administration that has entered into partnerships with several countries, some with human rights concerns, to take third-country removals from the U.S.
The Trump administration in May 2025 made an emergency request to the Supreme Court after U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy blocked the policy.
The Supreme Court in June 2025 temporarily allowed for the removals, before sending it back to the lower court.
The Trump administration later appealed to the First Circuit, and could appeal again to the Supreme Court.
text:
A federal appeals court Friday struck down the Trump administration’s policy to quickly send noncitizens to countries they are not from, finding that immigrants must have an opportunity to challenge their removal if they fear for their safety.

The decision largely upheld a Boston federal judge’s February ruling that found the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful. But the immigration officers can still conduct third-country removals if they follow the proper procedures, such as adequate notice and an opportunity for an immigrant to raise a fear-based claim to that country of removal.

Third-country removals, deportations from the United States to a nation other than an immigrant’s home country, occur when the immigrant’s home country does not accept the person’s repatriation.

Once rare, the procedure has spiked under the second Trump administration that has entered into partnerships with several countries, some with human rights concerns, to take third-country removals from the U.S.

The three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit also raised doubts that a country that accepts a person that is not their own citizen could “credibly provide blanket assurances that all removed noncitizens will not be persecuted or tortured there unless it intends to provide them with some sort of affirmative protection against rogue agents and non-state actors.”

The panel also upheld the lower court’s finding that the notice to a third country was inadequate — about 24 hours — and that the policy was unlawful.

It gives “no notice at all of an impending third-country removal when the country to which the noncitizen is to be removed has provided credible (in the State Department’s judgment) diplomatic assurances that noncitizens removed there from the United States will not be persecuted or tortured,” the panel wrote.

The panel included circuit judges Lara E. Montecalvo, Jeffrey R. Howard and Seth R. Aframe. Former President Joe Biden nominated Montecalvo and Aframe. Former President George W. Bush nominated Howard.

The Trump administration in May 2025 made an emergency request to the Supreme Court after U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy blocked the policy. The Supreme Court in June 2025 temporarily allowed for the removals, before sending it back to the lower court.

Murphy again in February issued an order that blocked the policy and required DHS to carry out the statutory obligations of proper notice of removal to a third country and to give a noncitizen enough time to raise any concerns for their safety to their removal to a third country.

The Trump administration later appealed to the First Circuit, and could appeal again to the Supreme Court.

DHS did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment Friday.

text:
A coalition of 15 press freedom advocacy organizations on Friday demanded the release of Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano, who was arrested by federal immigration enforcement officials earlier this week.

The groups—which include Free Press, the Committee to Protect Journalists, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the National Association of Hispanic Journalists, and Reporters Without Borders (RSF)—released a letter decrying Galeano's detention at the hands of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents on Monday.

The organizations expressed concern about Galeano being potentially deported back to Nicaragua, where he could face imprisonment for his past work exposing that government's human rights abuses. According to a Wednesday report in The Guardian, Galeano fled his home country eight years ago shortly after police raided the news outlet where he worked.

The groups also said Galeano's detention marked "a troubling escalation of attacks on journalists and media workers, particularly immigrant journalists, who consistently provide much-needed journalism and civic information for their communities."

Galeano was taken into custody despite entering the US legally in 2018 and having a pending asylum case. The Nicaraguan journalist also has a work permit and a Social Security number.

Nora Benavidez, senior counsel at Free Press, called Galeano's arrest "horrifying," while noting that the Nicaraguan is "the latest in a long line of journalists who came to the United States to report on issues of the day and instead face deportation."

"These cases aren’t just about cracking down on immigration," said Benavidez. "They are about cutting off community access to vital coverage and scaring reporters from holding those in power accountable. If our government can close off channels of exchange and the free flow of ideas, it is no more than a dictatorship."

Edith Rodríguez Cachera, vice president of RSF Spain, pointed out that Galeano was also a citizen of Spain, and urged the Spanish government to secure his freedom.

"Spain cannot stand by while one of its citizens, a journalist persecuted for doing his job, is detained in the United States and faces the risk of being sent back to a country he fled because of severe repression," said Rodríguez Cachera, "where his safety could be seriously endangered if he is deported. Spain must use every diplomatic and consular instrument at its disposal to safeguard his security and prevent his return to a country where he will likely be targeted due to his journalistic work."

Galeano's wife, Deykell Santamaría, said in an interview with El País published Thursday that she has been able to contact her husband during his detention, but she still fears "for his safety, his freedom, and his integrity if he were to be sent to Nicaragua."

Javier Melendez, a longtime friend of the detained journalist, was even blunter about what would happen to Galeano were he to be deported, describing it as nothing less than a "death sentence" in an interview with The Guardian.

The El País report noted that US Reps. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) and Mario Díaz-Balart (R-Fla.) have expressed concerns about Galeano's detention, with Salazar saying that the US government should "always know how to distinguish between a criminal and a political exile."
