text:
(CN) — Four men testifying Friday to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s arrest and detention practices in Oregon said they were asked few, if any, questions before they were taken to detention facilities hours away from their homes.

Speaking through Spanish interpreters, the men — all in their 20s and 30s who work in blue-collar and service-connected jobs — said they still fear arrest by ICE and potential deportation, despite the fact that they are following immigration laws.

Their testimony bolstered arguments from a class of Oregon immigrants who want U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai to ensure the government is complying with his February injunction preventing ICE agents from arresting Oregon residents without a warrant and without determining whether they posed a flight risk.

The order provided them with new rules and parameters for how to perform an arrest that comported with the law.

A 34-year-old man from Venezuela, known only as JCCV, living in The Dalles, Oregon, with his family, said that he had a pending immigration application when he was inexplicably detained and taken to a Portland facility for multiple days.

He said agents mistook him for his brother, who is also living in the U.S., but didn’t bother to check his identification.

JCCV and other witnesses described being pressured by agents into signing a document for voluntary self-deportation.

“Before you signed it, did anyone explain to you that you were signing a document that would cause you to be removed from the country?” Kasubhai asked the man.

“No,” he said.

“What documents were the language in?”

“English.”

“Can you read English?”

“No.”

“Would you have signed the documents if they told you it was a form for voluntary departure?”

“No.”

Nelly Paola Garcia Orjuela, an attorney with the Innovation Law Lab, said the warrantless arrests were part of the Trump administration’s efforts to hit immigration arrest quotas to conform with the president’s sweeping deportation program.

“This meant a contingent of ICE agents were deployed to arrest many Oregonians without a warrant, detain them and transfer them out of state. Defendants did not discontinue this practice, and it’s because defendants continue to defy the law and are not complying with the law is why we are here today," Orjuela said.

Specifically, Orjuela accused ICE of making flight risk assessments of arrestees after their detention, applying improper flight risk standards, underreporting arrests and redacting and withholding arrest data meant to ensure compliance with the judge’s order, among other things.

Amber Qureshi, an attorney with the Deportation Data Project, which publicizes immigration enforcement data through Freedom of Information Act requests and other sources, testified there were 574 immigration arrests in Oregon between the judge’s February order and July.

Of those, 504 have been noncustodial arrests, which means they are more likely to have occurred without an arrest warrant, she explained.

At the end of an all-day evidentiary hearing, the judge signaled support for the request.

“At the minimum, the attention behind the document disclosure ordered in the preliminary injunction is not being met,” Kasubhai, a Joe Biden appointee, said. “I need to revisit what is being required to ensure the respondents are complying with my preliminary injunction.”

On cross-examination, the DOJ attorneys attempted to poke holes in witness testimony, questioning the validity and consistency of their statements.

“Plaintiffs bear the burden of demonstrating defendants have the violated injunction by clear and convincing evidence. They have not met that burden," DOJ attorney Ariana Garousi said.

Department of Justice attorneys argued that the men all had warrants for their arrest, which necessitated their detention.

Kasubhai also expressed confusion over ICE’s use of previously issued warrants to re-arrest immigrants.

“The idea that a warrant is issued and then someone is taken into custody and released generally means that the warrant is now resolved, and if somebody wanted to take that individual back into custody there would have to be an issuance of another warrant,” he said. “That doesn’t mean that the underlying issue has been resolved, but a new warrant has to be issued.”

But the DOJ attorneys argued that is not what Department of Homeland Security regulations require.

DOJ attorneys only called one witness, an ICE agent in the Medford, Oregon, known as JG who described the arrest of two of the witnesses. The hearing will continue Monday.

text:
Costa Rican content creator Julián Valverde, known online as Julián Valjota, is in the custody of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. A source close to the case confirmed his custody, and said the 26-year-old, whose full name is José Julián Valverde Meneses, is being processed by US immigration authorities.

Costa Rican journalist Elías Alvarado confirmed on Thursday night that Valverde was detained on Wednesday, in Orlando, and the reasons have not been made public. Alvarado said people close to Valverde told him that Orlando police stopped the creator while he was driving.

Alvarado also said no official information yet establishes the circumstances of the detention, Valverde’s current immigration status, or whether he faces a final order of removal from the United States. Before the custody confirmation, Alvarado had said Valverde did not appear in ICE records.

The detention became public yesterday through fellow content creator Christopher Araya, known as Araya Vlogs. In a video, Araya said Valverde had been held for nearly 24 hours and had not yet appeared before a judge. He added that the group was in contact with Valverde’s attorney and with lawyers who specialize in immigration.

Araya said Valverde had asked him to share the news in order to head off rumors. Valverde’s last social media post, published Wednesday night, was a video recorded inside his car with a patrol vehicle visible behind him. Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it is following the case. The ministry’s Consular Department and the Consulate General in Miami said they are aware of the situation and are making inquiries with US immigration authorities to learn more about the citizen’s circumstances.

The case also reached the Legislative Assembly. Frente Amplio lawmaker Joselyn Sáenz called on the Foreign Ministry to act to protect Valverde and all Costa Ricans held by ICE in the United States. She also criticized ICE over what she described as alleged inhumane, degrading and discriminatory treatment.

Valverde has lived in the United States for more than five years and left Costa Rica in search of work opportunities. He has frequently joked in his content about a possible deportation, though those remarks do not establish his current immigration status or explain this week’s detention.

Costa Rica is among the countries whose citizens are subject to mandatory consular notification when arrested or detained in the United States. US authorities must therefore notify the relevant Costa Rican consulate without delay.

The next steps depend on facts not yet made public. If a final removal order exists, ICE could move ahead with his departure, including arranging travel documents. If he has an open immigration case, a pending protection claim or another legal avenue to challenge removal, his attorneys could pursue those remedies.

text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent told Newsweek she was effectively forced out of a job after reporting concerns about detention conditions and the way she was treated in the workplace through official whistleblower channels.

Lenicia Shannon, a 46-year-old deportation officer assigned to ICE's Miami Field Office in Stuart, Florida, said she reported alleged discrimination, harassment, misconduct, and detention-related concerns to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC), an independent federal watchdog responsible for protecting federal whistleblowers and investigating retaliation complaints.

She accused ICE of failing to adequately investigate complaints she filed with federal oversight bodies, and said the agency subsequently retaliated by issuing a Letter of Counseling, referring her for a fitness-for-duty evaluation, suspending her law-enforcement authority, and ultimately placing her on paid administrative leave.

Read More on U.S.

ICE records provided by Shannon and reviewed by Newsweek showed that the agency later accused Shannon of disruptive and combative conduct during a February 2026 reasonable-accommodation meeting, allegations she denies. Other records reviewed show that, before those actions, Shannon received multiple commendations, leadership recognitions, and awards from the agency.

"When you report it, you become a target," Shannon told Newsweek in an interview. "You’re the victim, and they make you the adversary."

When reached for comment on the allegations, a spokesperson for ICE told Newsweek, "In accordance with U.S. privacy laws, ICE does not publicly discuss the administrative matters of individual employees."

The agency did not confirm or deny Shannon's claims.

Complaints Dating Back Years

Shannon says she spent years filing complaints through multiple channels. She says some went to OSC, while others were submitted to ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility and the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General.

She said her dispute with the agency began in November 2022, when she filed an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging discrimination, harassment and a hostile work environment involving her then-supervisor. She said her complaints centered on her treatment as a Black woman in the organization.

Shannon said she initially attempted to address the issues internally but believed ICE did not properly follow its procedures for handling workplace harassment.

She noted that the anti-harassment policy required reporting to a supervisor, but noted that the supervisor was the person she alleged had harassed her.

After approximately 10 months, she said the agency transferred her out of the supervisor's unit.

Emails obtained by Newsweek show that by early 2025, Shannon repeatedly asked management to intervene, objecting to reporting through her supervisor's chain of command while EEO complaints remained pending, and saying the ongoing dispute was affecting her well-being and work environment.

In a June 2025 whistleblower disclosure, Shannon alleged that agency leadership repeatedly failed to address her concerns of discrimination, harassment, and a hostile work environment. She also alleged that officials permitted her supervisor to serve in acting leadership positions despite pending EEO complaints involving him.

According to the disclosure, Shannon complained that the supervisor hung an image in a communal workspace depicting a black lion surrounded by white sheep with blue eyes, which she said she found offensive. Shannon said she viewed the image as intimidating.

"That is intimidation," Shannon said. "It makes me feel uncomfortable."

Shannon said she sought counseling and repeatedly attempted to resolve the situation internally.

Detention Concerns from ICE Officer

In a June 29, 2025, OSC disclosure, Shannon alleged that ICE's Miami Area of Responsibility had begun housing detainees overnight in temporary office space that lacked beds, showers, medical staff, and adequate emergency capabilities. She characterized the practice as an abuse of authority and named several ICE managers whom she believed were responsible.

"The facility is only authorized for short-term temporary holding, yet now being used outside it's intended and regulated purpose, placing both detainees and staff at risk of legal liability and risk," Shannon wrote in one OSC disclosure.

"It lacks the infrastructure and resources for overnight detention, placing both detainees and staff at significant risk."

Another disclosure filed on September 28 alleged that detainees were being held beyond the expiration of ICE detainers and rebooked into custody under new holds.

"It has come to my attention and direct observation that detainees—primarily female individuals—are routinely held in local custody for 72 hours or longer after the expiration of ICE detainers, in violation of federal law and established constitutional standards."

The filings show Shannon reported several concerns; however, they do not establish whether OSC substantiated them.

An ICE spokesperson said the agency is "committed to ensuring that all those in its custody reside in safe, secure, and humane environments under appropriate conditions of confinement."

"The agency takes misconduct allegations very seriously—personnel are held to the highest standards of professional and ethical behavior, and when a complaint is received, it is investigated thoroughly to determine veracity and ensure comprehensive standards are strictly maintained and enforced."

"I believe that people who violate the immigration laws, I have to deport them," she said. "But I don't have to disrespect people and violate anybody's rights doing it for statistics and for numbers."

An ICE spokesperson said the agency encourages employees and detainees to report concerns through multiple oversight channels, including the DHS Office of Inspector General, ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility and the Detention Reporting and Information Line.

Counseling and Fitness Review

In a September 2025 email complaint, Shannon said that an ICE firearms instructor called her a "crazy b****" and threatened to "let me have it" over a dispute.

On September 24, 2025, ICE issued Shannon a Letter of Counseling citing workplace incidents that the agency characterized as disruptive or unprofessional. The document says that it was not disciplinary action and would not be placed in her official personnel file. Shannon later described the counseling as retaliatory.

The dispute escalated to a fitness-for-duty review, she said.

A fitness-for-duty letter reviewed by Newsweek says that ICE sought medical information regarding Shannon's ability to perform law-enforcement duties. Separate medical documentation from a healthcare provider later said that Shannon was medically fit for duty without restrictions.

In a February 2026 retaliation complaint filed with OSC, Shannon argued that the counseling and fitness-for-duty process was initiated because she had reported misconduct through official channels.

That complaint named an acting field office director, a supervisory detention and deportation officer, and a supervisory detention and deportation officer as officials Shannon alleged were involved in retaliatory actions following her whistleblower disclosures.

Administrative Leave

Internal agency records show that Shannon was placed on paid administrative leave on February 27, 2026, for what ICE called "allegations of misconduct."

In a subsequent retaliation complaint, Shannon said the agency told her the action stemmed from allegations that she was combative, created a safety concern, and engaged in disruptive conduct during a February 26 reasonable-accommodation meeting. She denies those allegations.

Agency records show that ICE suspended her authority to carry agency-approved firearms and required her to surrender law-enforcement equipment.

A March 2 OSC filing challenged those actions and alleged that the agency removed her credentials, weapon, overtime opportunities, and operational duties because of her whistleblower activity.

In August 2026, the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General's Whistleblower Protection Division declined to investigate Shannon's retaliation complaint and advised her to pursue the matter through OSC and other administrative channels.

Records reviewed by Newsweek show that Shannon received multiple commendations and professional recognitions during her six years with ICE, including a January 2023 commendation for border operations in Laredo, a May 2023 appreciation letter for a New Orleans assignment, a DHS leadership recognition letter and a Director's Award for Distinguished Service in 2023, as well as completion of agency mentoring and leadership-development programs in 2024 and 2025.

Surveillance Allegations Remain Unsubstantiated

Shannon also alleges that federal personnel improperly monitored her devices and private communications.

Records reviewed by Newsweek show she repeatedly reported those concerns to OPR, OIG, OSC, and local police, alleging that surveillance technology had been used against her.

She also said that co-workers repeatedly recited private home telephone conversations back to her.

"They started repeating phone conversations of mine," Shannon alleged. "Like if I would talk to my mom at home, somebody would come in and talk about something that we spoke about…and laugh in my face."

According to a July 2025 Port St. Lucie Police Department report, Shannon told officers she believed someone was illegally surveilling her cellphone and may have entered her home without permission. She reported phone issues including overheating, battery drain and unusual sounds during calls, as well as unexplained tire tracks in her garage and suspected tobacco spit at her residence.

The report documented her allegations but identified no suspect and found no evidence connecting any person to the reported incidents.

An independent forensic review of Shannon's phone found no spyware, malware, stalkerware, or unauthorized VPN. The examiner found unidentified Bluetooth records and recommended additional review, but did not determine that the device had been hacked or connect any activity to any federal agency.

Shannon also reported to police in Montgomery, Alabama, that two laptops and an iPad stored inside a signal-blocking bag were stolen from the trunk of her vehicle.

'Rights Violated'

Shannon, a breast cancer survivor who underwent surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation before joining ICE on a medical waiver, expressed frustration with her treatment.

"My rights have been egregiously violated, and after fighting for my life, this agency and its racist practices are disturbing and illegal."

"I worked really hard for this job," she said. "I don't think that these are the values and the morals and the integrity of the agency from where I started six years ago."

Shannon alleged that Black women in the agency faced harsher consequences than male colleagues accused of more serious misconduct, saying they were stripped of credentials, equipment, and workplace access over comparatively minor administrative allegations.

"The sequence and disparity raise serious concerns that administrative allegations are being used as a mechanism to discredit the reporting officer," she said, adding that the treatment sent "a chilling message to any employee who considers reporting misconduct, harassment, or discrimination within the agency."

text:
Christian Castro, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot a man through the door of a north Minneapolis home in January, was released Thursday evening on conditional bail from Hennepin County Jail, where he was held for state-level charges.

At his first appearance at federal district court in St. Paul on Friday for a separate case, Castro pleaded not guilty to six charges of making false statements, stemming from six alleged lies he told FBI investigators after the shooting.

Castro had appeared in state court in downtown Minneapolis Thursday to face state charges of four counts of second-degree assault as well as one count of falsely reporting a crime.

ICE agent in Jan. 14 Minneapolis shooting makes first appearance in Minnesota state court

On Jan. 14, during the peak of Operation Metro Surge, Castro engaged in a car chase with Alfredo Aljorna, ending at Aljorna’s home in north Minneapolis. Castro and another ICE agent had mistaken Aljorna for another Latino man, according to an FBI affidavit. Aljorna exited his car and slipped as he tried to get inside his house, at which point Castro attempted to arrest Aljorna. Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, Aljorna’s roommate, tried to help Aljorna, leading to an 11-second scuffle between the three. After both men escaped and ran inside, Castro shot at them with the bullet passing through the front door and hitting Sosa-Celis in the leg before coming to a stop in the wall of a child’s bedroom, according to charging documents.

In an interview in the aftermath of the shooting, Castro told an FBI agent that Sosa-Celis and Aljorna had assaulted him with a broom and a snow shovel in a three-minute fight before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.

State prosecutors charged Castro in May, and a federal grand jury indicted him in early September. An assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota had been pursuing hefty federal civil rights charges against Castro, but was instructed by Justice Department officials in Washington, D.C. to downgrade the charges. The attorney was then fired, CBS News reported, citing four unnamed sources familiar with the matter.

The state and federal cases are taking place simultaneously. Castro, who had refused to consent to extradition to Minnesota from a Texas jail for months, turned himself in to federal authorities in early September after a federal grand jury indicted him with the six charges. He was released on bond after appearing in federal court in McAllen, Texas, and ordered to appear in federal court in Minnesota for the Friday hearing. Castro drove up to Minnesota from Texas this week, where he was arrested Wednesday in downtown Minneapolis by the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension.

On Thursday, Hennepin County District Judge Paul R. Scoggin set bail at $200,000 if Castro agrees to not possess firearms, not contact witnesses, to be electronically monitored, to sign a waiver of extradition — an agreement to be extradited without a formal hearing in the future — and to surrender his passport to state authorities immediately if he gets it back from federal authorities.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said that she expects Castro to file a motion to move the state case to federal court, which she said her office is prepared to litigate.

Castro was released on conditional bail from state custody at around 6 p.m. Thursday, according to the Hennepin County Sheriff’s jail roster. He wore a black suit and an ankle monitor to federal court Friday, a stark difference from the day prior, when he was still in state custody and appeared in state court in a glass-paneled box and an orange jail uniform.

text:
By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) – A US federal appeals court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by President Donald Trump’s administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.

Ruling in a case ​that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US ‌Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful.

The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

“This decision confirms that ‌due process ​and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented ⁠by putting someone on a plane ⁠to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings,” Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said

Under Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, ​in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal. Earlier in the same case, the administration twice convinced the ⁠Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants’ due process rights, clearing ⁠the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

DHS had no ​immediate comment.

Under the third-country deportation program, DHS adopted a policy in March 2025 that would allow migrants to be sent to ​such countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted ‌or tortured there.

The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.

THIRD COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS

US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect migrants’ due process rights and could ⁠lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous countries, without notice.

On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy’s order if left intact would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to ⁠third countries.

But US Circuit Judge Seth ‌Aframe, writing for Friday’s panel, said Murphy adopted a “sensible” interpretation of the immigration ⁠law requiring migrants be given a “meaningful” chance to raise any concerns before they ​are deported.

“DHS’s ‌proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of ​noncitizens who ⁠are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” Aframe wrote. “We decline to adopt such an interpretation.”

The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, and a judge appointed by a Republican president.

However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy’s ruling on procedural grounds. That part of the ruling concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third countries.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in ​Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

description:

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed claims that ICE enforcement tactics led to reduced employment in cities where arrests spiked.

text:
Employment fell last year in U.S. cities where Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests surged the most, according to a recent study.

In cities where ICE arrests increased fastest in 2025, employment fell 0.4% below its expected trajectory both immediately after those detentions and for up to one year after a metro area was targeted, researchers with the Brookings Institution said in the report. On average, each arrest in cities where ICE's presence significantly increased was associated with four lost jobs, the nonpartisan think tank said.

"We found that employment fell in the cities where ICE activity surged, and not just among immigrants, but there were broader effects, including for Americans," Marcela Escobari, the report's lead author and a former special assistant to the White House National Security Council during the Biden administration, told CBS News.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed claims that ICE enforcement tactics led to reduced employment in cities where arrests spiked.

"The surge in illegal immigration under President Biden threatened the long-run fiscal health of the country, contributed to record high inflation and suppressed the wages of American workers," she said in a statement to CBS News. "There is no shortage of American minds and hands to grow our labor force, and President Trump's agenda to create jobs for American workers represents this Administration's commitment to capitalizing on that untapped potential while delivering on our mandate to enforce our immigration laws."

Border security has been a top priority during the second Trump administration. Stronger immigration enforcement policies "protect American workers, reduce strain on local communities, and reinforce the nation's right to control its borders and determine who enters the United States," according to a White House statement.

The Trump administration ramped up its immigration crackdown in 2025. In January, thousands of federal agents were deployed to Minneapolis-St. Paul to investigate alleged fraud, leading to mass protests and the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal officers.

In July, ICE detentions set a monthly record high for Mr. Trump's second term, with the agency taking into custody more than 46,000 individuals facing deportation because of alleged immigration violations, like entering the U.S. illegally or overstaying their visas, CBS News has reported.

Businesses disrupted

Increased ICE arrests in U.S. cities last year drove job losses in three ways, Escobari told CBS News. First, some workers stopped reporting for work because they feared encountering ICE.

"Fear drove workers to withdraw from the labor force even when they weren't arrested," she said.

This led to labor disruptions for some businesses, leading them to reduce their operating hours, delay expansion, freeze hiring, or, in some cases, lay off staff or shut down, according to Brookings.

"We spoke to people in the field who explicitly said, if their framing crew is led by immigrants and they stop working or get arrested, they can't hand off the project to their roofing crew, and the project stalls," Escobari said, referring to the impact of increased ICE enforcement in the construction sector. "The company still needs to pay its debts, and many close altogether. When they close, the project manager or equipment operator and other occupations that tend to be occupied by American workers also lose their jobs."

Rising ICE arrests in cities in 2025 also reduced employment by sapping consumer demand and spending, hurting local businesses, according to the Brookings researchers.

"These [ICE] operations engender widespread fear, and when people stop going out, they stop spending, and that forces businesses to close," Escobari said.

Other research has also found a negative impact of increased ICE enforcement on local economies. A 2026 study from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania found that economic activity and consumer spending dropped last year in metro areas where ICE conducted raids.

"Effects intensify near raid sites, do not dissipate over time and are remarkably general: Declines occur regardless of neighborhood demography, affect workplaces and consumer-facing stores across myriad industries, and trigger no substitution to online shopping," Exequiel Hernandez, an expert on global and corporate strategy, wrote. "The breadth of the local economic damage mirrors the breadth of the enforcement approach."

Anti-ICE protesters are planning a demonstration near the South Arlington home of a top federal official tomorrow (Saturday).

A vigil and procession taking aim at ICE tactics, federal immigration policy and the actions of Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, are expected to take place in Alcova Heights.

The protest is the latest in a series of actions targeting the Arlington homes of figures associated with the Trump administration.

Faith leaders and other organizers plan to pass near Vought’s home and place stones around the neighborhood with the names of people who have died in ICE detention.

“Today we remember the lives lost by utter neglect, lack of human dignity, senseless and brutal violence carried out by the hands and weapons of ICE agents,” organizers said in a press release. “As a community, together we must dismantle the lies, seek the truth, and demand justice from those who are causing this harm. Never again is now.”

The action follows a sidewalk chalk protest outside the home of White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller in September 2025 and a noisy demonstration outside the North Arlington home of the CEO of Hilton Hotels in February.

More recently, anti-ICE protesters gathered outside the Arlington County Justice Center last month in support of a man who says he suffered a brain bleed after ICE officers reportedly chased him and shot him with a Taser in a parking lot on Columbia Pike.

A man was also arrested on an attempted murder charge earlier this year after he allegedly showed up at Vought’s home while armed in August 2025.

Speakers at this weekend’s vigil will include Rev. Julio Hernandez of the Congregation Action Network, Rabbi Jeffrey Saxe of Temple Rodef Shalom and Rev. Carol Thomas Cissel of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Arlington.

“This regime has been detaining immigrants and holding them in for-profit prison camps,” Eli Tabb, an organizer with the Refugee and Immigrant Solidarity Coalition, said. “ICE agents and other deputized law enforcement personnel are killing innocent non-violent civilians on the street and in these camps, all under the guise of immigration enforcement.”

The protest is scheduled to begin at Alcova Heights Park at 2 p.m. and conclude with “a slow and peaceful procession” stopping “near” Vought’s home.
